item.title: The Therapy of Art
item.description:
Creativity

The Therapy of Art

Personal Perspective: Access to the artist can change the experience of a work.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • Interpreting a painting is similar to a therapist interpreting a patient’s behaviors and beliefs.
  • Hearing about the artist’s motivations and intentions from the artist adds to the experience of the artwork.
  • The Other Art Fair rewards the woman who has something to say and refuses to sit behind her own canvas.

“I remember being at a dinner party a while back and there was an abstract painting on the wall. I kind of liked it. Whatever you’re supposed to get from art, it was happening. And the host of the party came up to me and he said, “A machine painted that.” And I was impressed with the technology, but whatever I was feeling about that painting was gone.” — Aaron Sorkin, New York Times, September 27, 2026

In a 1969 lecture published under the title “What Is an Author?”, French philosopher Michel Foucault rhetorically asked if we should include Nietzsche’s laundry list in his body of work to help interpret some of his masterpieces. The question for us is: Should an artist’s verbal or written articulations about their motivation and intention be considered when viewing an artwork?

I believe that firsthand knowledge of the artist’s motivations and intentions adds to the experience of an artwork, and that is why The Other Art Fair is my favorite art fair: because there is something somewhat rogue about standing in front of an artwork with the artist herself, hearing directly from her about her motivations and intentions as well as the process and technique, rather than making an interpretation from our own isolated perspective. Access to the artist changes the experience of the work entirely, and I find that it makes the viewing far richer than it would otherwise be. It also means that the art fair rewards precisely the kind of woman who has something to say and refuses to stay quietly behind her own canvas.

Touring The Other Art Fair this weekend, I first spoke with Hannah Gilson about her painting “Knowledge” that depicts the books she wants her daughter to read; however, these are books that do not exist (yet). Hannah explained to me that the traditional literary canon, the books most of us were assigned in high school and college, no longer serves everyone (which is why the literary canon that I studied at university in the 1980s is now often referred to as that of “Dead White Males”). And although similar existential, psychological, and moral questions persist today, it is time to allow new voices to wrestle with these themes regarding what it means to be human. I found something wonderfully irreverent about “Knowledge,” learning that a mother preferred to imagine enlightening titles than hand her daughter antiquated knowledge.

"Knowledge"
Source: Hannah Gilson

Next I spoke with Halle Ross about “Trust, but Verify,” and she told me that the painting “was created as a reminder to trust in the larger unfolding of life and the possibility that things work out, even when the path forward is unclear. The work reflects the balance between surrender and discernment, trusting the process while remaining engaged with the reality in front of us.” I loved Halle’s explication and thought it was representative of how I suggest patients approach life: that we need to show up authentically and with discernment but without prejudice. We shouldn’t try to figure out everything in advance and instead try to endure uncertainty, which is often quite difficult.

article continues after advertisement
Source: Halle Ross

Lastly, I spoke with Isabel Maddahi about her painting "The Big One,” and she told me, “For a few months, I found myself blocked. I knew what I was feeling, but I struggled to put it into words. It was always, ‘It's this, but not quite that.’ One day I went home and simply started painting, without a plan or expectation, and let what I was feeling internally take shape on the canvas.”

This reminded me of what makes art therapeutic, namely that it offers a non-verbal language for emotions and overwhelming sensations that may be beyond words. Isabel’s rebelliousness is against language itself, against the pressure to arrive at a tidy and contained verbal account of her interior life. I found something quietly radical in Isabel’s decision to let this canvas speak “The Big One.”

"The Big One"
Source: Isabel Maddahi

Speaking with each of these women turbo-charged my sense of wonder regarding how artistic expression is therapeutic. The opportunity to stand shoulder to shoulder with the actual creators and ask them about their motivations and intentions gave me new insights into what they hope viewers will feel.

Interpreting a painting is similar to a therapist interpreting a patient’s behaviors and beliefs, piecing a puzzle together, trying to determine what caused the artist to express herself in this manner. Art can show us what is in our blind spots the same way that therapists can—“To hold, as ‘twere, the mirror up to nature,” as Shakespeare wrote.

article continues after advertisement

The type of inside access to artists that The Other Art Fair facilitates is thrilling. I found Hannah’s distrust of the traditional literary canon to be justified; I found Halle’s account of trusting an unclear path while maintaining discernment to be courageous; and I found Isabel’s expressing her emotions through colors and forms instead of words to be edifying.

To respond to Foucault, I’m not sure that I need to know anything about the artists’ laundry lists, but having their thoughts about motivation and intention freely offered while standing in front of their work is very inspiring.

item.title: Family Estrangement: Are Therapists Part of the Problem?
item.description:
Family Dynamics

Family Estrangement: Are Therapists Part of the Problem?

When clients consider estrangement, therapists must examine their influence.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • Family estrangement is on the rise.
  • Therapists may inadvertently contribute to relationship rupture.
  • As a profession, we need to examine whether our strategies are in our clients' long-term best interests.
Family Estrangement: Are we part of the problem?
Source: Picmedia / Creative Commons

A recent Wall Street Journal article entitled “Are Therapists to Blame for the Rise in Adults Cutting Off Their Parents?” brought renewed attention to the growing number of adult children who are ending relationships with their parents and to a recent conference—The Family Summit—that was devoted to this painful family phenomenon.

As a keynote speaker at the conference, I want to share one troubling moment that deserves particular attention from those of us in the mental health profession.

As a therapist who has spent nearly five decades helping people repair relationships that seemed beyond hope, I have been deeply troubled by the growing number of people who are choosing emotional cutoffs as a way of dealing with difficult relationships.

Although some abusive relationships undoubtedly warrant distance—or even termination—people are now severing ties for reasons that, in the past, might have been regarded as annoying, painful, or intrusive, but certainly not as cause for terminating a relationship.

Although these “relationship sabbaticals” may provide some immediate relief, rarely do they take into account lasting emotional consequences that extend far beyond the two people involved, affecting siblings, spouses, children, grandchildren, and generations to come.

You didn’t have to be a therapist to feel the palpable pain of those attending the Family Summit Conference in Chicago—mostly parents of adult children who were no longer in contact with them. In my nearly 50 years as a therapist and conference speaker, I have rarely witnessed such profound grief concentrated in one room.

Most troubling, however, was the response I received after asking the audience a question: “How many of you believe that a therapist contributed to your family’s estrangement?”

Most of the hands in the room went up. Those raised hands revealed how many parents truly believe that therapy played a significant role in their family ruptures.

When I expressed anger about times therapy is hurtful rather than helpful—ending rather than mending relationships—the sustained applause caught me off-guard.

Although it might be tempting to think, “These parents are defensive, or they lack understanding for their children’s legitimate concerns, or they’re just trying to blame their unhappiness on someone or something else,” I’m convinced we cannot dismiss the meaning of this show of hands.

It’s time to take a hard look at how we might be contributing to the escalating tendency to condone or even encourage unnecessary relationship rupture.

Most therapists don’t intentionally contribute to the breakdown in relationships, but I believe that certain clinical missteps can endanger already fragile connections. Here are several issues therapists should consider when working with this vulnerable population:

Recognize that all therapy, including our own, is biased

There is no such thing as neutral therapy. Regardless of a therapist’s degree or clinical orientation, what clients get when they go to therapy is the “person” behind the professional training. Our experiences, values, and beliefs influence what we notice, what is ignored, which possibilities are explored, and which are overlooked. Therapists channel conversations and often shape the conclusions clients reach.

For example, people in my couples practice often begin by saying, “The only reason I agreed to come is because we have kids. If it weren’t for them, I wouldn’t be here.”

Some therapists respond, “That isn’t a good enough reason to stay. Your children will leave home someday.”

My response is different: “The fact that you’re here because of your children tells me how much you love them and how important their well-being is to you. Where did you learn the importance of family?”

This reframes their shared love for their children as a strength and a reasonable place to begin—not as evidence that they are betraying themselves or settling for less than they deserve.

Same couple. Same facts. Different lens. Different conversation. And often, a different future.

Therapists should be transparent about the perspectives they bring to their work. Do they view ending an important relationship as a reasonable response to emotional discomfort? Or do they believe that most strained relationships deserve a wholehearted attempt at repair before cutoff is even considered?

Don’t Let One Side of the Story Determine What Happens Next

When someone complains to a friend about a parent, the friend is likely to say, “Your mother is so unreasonable,” or “I can’t believe your father did that.” Friends take our side. They are our allies.

Too often, the same thing happens in therapy. We care about our clients, hear their pain, and want to protect them from further hurt. So, we validate their feelings. And the narrative about parents’ wrongdoings continues, as labels such as “toxic,” “narcissistic,” “abusive,” or “gaslighting” are introduced into the conversation.

These labels then become the lens through which present and past interactions get viewed. When this happens, blame hardens, hope dims, and little is learned about navigating challenging relationships.

Instead, in addition to validating feelings, we need to make sure we have a thorough understanding of parents’ objectionable actions. When clients say, “My mother is controlling” or “My parents have always been abusive,” therapists should ask for specifics: “What has your mother actually done that felt controlling?” or “What do you mean by abusive? What exactly happened?”

Once the objectionable behavior is clear, it’s important to identify what clients have actually said and done to improve things, as well as the parents’ reactions. Figuring out which strategies simply aren’t effective and which may still have potential is key.

We also need to make sure that our clients are equipped with adequate communication skills before embarking on relationship repair—expressing feelings calmly using “I-messages,” discussing concrete, non-negotiable expectations without reiterating past transgressions, learning self-soothing strategies when triggered, and so on.

Additionally, helping adult children obtain a deeper understanding of what shaped their parent (though never a justification for hurtful behavior) can create empathy, which remains a cornerstone in any relationship that works.

Finally, mental health professionals must stop diagnosing people they have never met!

Hearing one person’s account about an absent parent’s behavior tells us nothing about that parent’s willingness to accept personal responsibility or their ability to change.

Absent imminent danger or ongoing abuse, therapists should exhaust the possibilities of repair before considering ending family relationships. Also, the parent should be invited to participate in joint sessions. If relationship therapy falls outside the therapist’s expertise, a referral to a qualified colleague is in order.

In the late 1980s, having witnessed the devastating effects of rampant divorce and the rise of disposable marriages, I took what was then an unorthodox stand in my book Divorce Busting: Most divorces are unnecessary.

Today, as family estrangement becomes increasingly normalized, complacency is once again not an option for me. It is time for therapists to examine the assumptions we bring into the therapy room and use our undeniable influence to help people establish healthy boundaries, navigate messy relationships, and—whenever possible—preserve connections with the family members who love them.

item.title: What Children’s Lies Tell Us About Development
item.description:
Deception

What Children’s Lies Tell Us About Development

Children's deception offers clues about cognitive, social, and moral growth.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • Lying requires children to understand that others can hold false beliefs.
  • Children's ability to lie improves as their social-cognitive skills develop.
  • Some childhood lies reflect growing empathy and concern for others' feelings.

I remember coming into the kitchen and finding the four-year-old standing there, making an effort to look innocent. Smeared across his face were chocolate and crumbs from an illicit cookie he had snuck. The seven-year-old had managed to sneak away before I came into the kitchen, but I could see where he had put the chair up against the cupboard to climb up to reach the cookies and hand them down to his brother.

I said, somewhat pointlessly as I already knew the answer, “Have you been eating cookies?”

The answer was no, with a hopeful shaking of the head. Maybe I would believe him?!

I didn’t, and I followed up with “Those oatmeal cookies are out of bounds before dinner.”

And he replied earnestly, “It wasn’t oatmeal!” Aha, no, it was chocolate cookies instead.

If you are a parent, you likely have had a similar experience. Most parents worry when they discover their child has lied. Lying is not something we want our children to do, especially to us. Sometimes parents are concerned that it may be a sign of a behavior problem or of poor character.

But developmental psychologists see something more than misbehavior. Children’s lies can provide valuable clues about their cognitive, social, and moral development. Understanding why children lie, and how deception changes with age, can help adults respond more effectively and support healthy development.

Why lying is harder than it looks

In fact, lying requires quite sophisticated thinking about others, the world, and how to control one’s behavior to influence others. Like the four-year-old, they can say things that contradict the false denial (“It wasn’t oatmeal”) or reveal information that arouses suspicion. To tell a convincing lie, children must understand that another person can hold a belief that differs from reality. They must keep track of what is true and what they have said so they do not contradict themselves or reveal the truth. Research has shown that children who are more advanced in these perspective-taking abilities are often better able to deceive successfully (Talwar & Lee, 2008).

As children grow, so do their lies

As children grow, their social-cognitive skills improve and, as a result, so does their ability to lie. While preschool children’s lies are often simple and easy to detect, older children become more sophisticated in their deception.

Later, asking the seven-year-old why the chair was against the cupboard, he answered, “I wanted to see what was for dinner.” Cute. Not likely, but he was trying to give a plausible explanation. It wasn’t a bad try. He was beginning to think about what I knew and tailoring his explanation accordingly.

article continues after advertisement

In fact, throughout the school years, children’s social-cognitive skills are improving, as does their ability to lie plausibly and maintain their lies (Evans & Lee, 2013; Talwar & Lee, 2008). While it can be easier to detect younger children’s lies, by early adolescence, many lies become much harder to detect.

However, developing the ability to lie does not mean children become chronic liars. Most, like adults, are predominantly honest. As children mature, they become better able to weigh when honesty is important and when competing social concerns are at stake.

As perspective-taking skills, empathy, and social understanding develop, children learn the downside of this newfound skill and deploy it more sparingly. They may choose to lie more strategically, including for prosocial reasons. For instance, our research has found that older children are more likely to hide disappointment about an unwanted gift out of concern for the gift-giver’s feelings, even when doing so comes at a cost to themselves (Talwar, Murphy & Lee, 2007; Popliger, Talwar & Crossman, 2011).

What children’s lies reveal about moral growth

Lying can tell us about moral development. Children do not learn about honesty on their own. They are taught the importance of honesty through witnessing others lie and tell the truth and the resulting consequences. Children gradually learn social expectations about honesty through conversations and interactions with their parents, teachers, peers, and others. They begin to navigate competing values, such as the desire to be honest but also kind and loyal, to help others but also protect themselves. Their lies often reveal how they are reasoning about these competing demands.

This does not mean that adults should encourage lying. Most of us value honesty, and lying remains a behavior we generally discourage. But when a child lies, it can be helpful to look beyond the behavior itself. Children’s lies can offer a window into how they think, understand others, and navigate their social world.

Understanding that lying is part of typical development raises another question: What do adults tend to get wrong about children’s lies? In future posts, I’ll examine five common misconceptions that shape how parents and educators respond when children are dishonest.

item.title: Involuntary Hospitalization vs. Involuntary Treatment
item.description:
Psychiatry

Involuntary Hospitalization vs. Involuntary Treatment

Legal-ethical struggles to protect autonomy in involuntary psychiatric care.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • People who pose serious imminent risks to themselves or others may be involuntarily hospitalized.
  • Involuntary hospitalization does not necessarily mean treatments can be imposed without consent.
  • Hospitalized patients have a right to make their own treatment decisions, provided they have mental capacity.
  • Psychologists should balance safety, client autonomy, doing good, avoiding harm, and due process.

When people experiencing a mental health crisis pose a serious, imminent risk to themselves or others, they may be hospitalized for a defined period of time without their consent. Although the precise standards vary by jurisdiction, involuntary hospitalization is generally intended to provide an opportunity to ensure immediate safety, allow time to evaluate the patient’s needs and risk, and stabilize the patient during a period of crisis.

Taking away someone’s freedom is an extraordinary exercise of state power. Accordingly, the goals of preventing harm and providing care must be balanced against autonomy: the right to make decisions about one’s own life, body, and medical or mental health treatment (Barsky, 2023).

A crucial distinction that sometimes gets lost in this discussion is that legal authorization to hospitalize a person involuntarily does not necessarily constitute authorization to treat that person without their consent. The legal standards for involuntary hospitalization, decision-making capacity, emergency intervention, and treatment over objection may be different.

Even when hospitalization is justified, patients should retain as much control as possible over such matters as medication, therapy, communication with family, cultural or spiritual support, daily routines, and discharge planning.

Mental Illness Does Not Automatically Mean Incapacity

People sometimes assume that involuntary hospitalization necessarily means that the patient lacks decision-making capacity. This assumption is incorrect. From a legal perspective, capacity depends on the particular decision to be made, at a particular time. A person may have difficulty making one type of decision while remaining capable of making others. Capacity can also fluctuate as symptoms, medications, sleep, stress, drug use, or medical conditions change.

Depending on particular state laws, assessing mental capacity for treatment decisions typically involves determining whether patients have the ability to:

  • understand information about their situation and treatment options;
  • appreciate how that information applies to their situation;
  • reason about their treatment options (given the benefits and risks of each); and
  • communicate a choice (Mather et al., 2025).

Although a diagnosis of schizophrenia, dementia, or another disorder may affect a person’s capacity, a diagnosis by itself does not establish incapacity. Clinicians must examine how specific symptoms such as hallucinations, delusions, depression, mania, or cognitive impairment are affecting the person’s capacity to make a particular type of treatment decision. Clinicians cannot determine mental incapacity simply because they or the patient’s family members disagree with the patient’s treatment choices.

Balancing Safety, Autonomy, and Other Interests

When serving involuntary patients, clinicians need to balance the interests of patient autonomy (freedom), beneficence (doing good), nonmaleficence (avoiding harm), and justice (treating people fairly), while addressing power imbalances and improving communication with patients (Laureano et al., 2024).

Professional ethics codes in psychology, counseling, and social work support informed consent and respect for self-determination (ACA, 2014; APA, 2017; NASW, 2021). These principles do not prohibit every intervention without consent, but they do require clinicians to justify any limitation on patient autonomy.

Substitute Decision Making

When a patient lacks decision-making capacity, state laws may authorize a legally recognized substitute (such as a healthcare agent, guardian, or family member) to make decisions on the patient’s behalf (Barsky, 2023). Substitute decision makers ordinarily should follow the patient’s wishes and values, rather than simply choosing what the substitute personally prefers.

In emergencies, clinicians may sometimes intervene without prior authorization to prevent immediate and serious harm. Emergency authority, however, should not become a blanket justification for continuing treatment over objection after the emergency has passed.

Laws governing involuntary treatment vary substantially by state, treatment setting, and type of intervention. Under the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments of the U.S. Constitution, individuals cannot be deprived of their liberty “without due process of the law.” For instance, the U.S. Supreme Court has recognized a constitutionally protected liberty interest in avoiding the unwanted administration of antipsychotic medication, although that interest may be overridden under particular circumstances and with appropriate procedural safeguards (Riggins v. Nevada, 1992; Washington v. Harper, 1990). The due process clauses also apply to individuals who have been incarcerated due to criminal convictions (State ex rel. Urban v. Hardy, 2025).

Effects of Coerced Treatment

On the positive side, involuntary care can protect life and create an opportunity for recovery. Unfortunately, it can also be frightening, humiliating, or traumatic, particularly when patients do not understand what is happening or believe that staff are ignoring their concerns.

In a recent research review, Corderoy et al. (2025) found mixed evidence concerning the impact of involuntary inpatient treatment. Some patients experienced clinical improvement or protection from immediate danger, while others reported coercion, loss of trust, trauma, or reluctance to seek future care. Research involving patients and nurses likewise highlights the power imbalances, uncertainty, and loss of control that patients may experience during involuntary care (Pariseau-Legault et al., 2025). Patients are more likely to experience psychiatric care as respectful and less coercive when professionals explain decisions, listen to their concerns, involve them meaningfully in decision-making, and offer choices and less restrictive alternatives whenever possible (Silva et al., 2023).

Protecting Patient Rights During Involuntary Hospitalization

If you or someone you know is concerned about involuntary hospitalization or treatment, ask the facility to explain the legal basis for the hospitalization, whether the patient has been assessed for treatment capacity, which treatments are being proposed, and why. If the patient has mental capacity, the patient should be allowed to refuse proposed treatments and request alternatives.

If you need assistance, ask how to contact a patient-rights advocate, ombudsperson, ethics consultation service, or legal representative. You could also ask how to request a hearing, review, second opinion, or appeal.

Procedures and rights vary by jurisdiction. An attorney or disability-rights organization familiar with local mental health law may be needed when there is a dispute about mental capacity and involuntary treatment.

Involuntary Treatment as a Last Resort

Involuntary hospitalization and treatment may sometimes be necessary to prevent serious harm. Still, coercive interventions should be used only when legally authorized, clinically necessary, proportionate to the danger, and less restrictive options are inadequate.

Whenever possible, professionals should try to prevent crises through voluntary services, collaborative safety planning, psychiatric advance directives, supported decision-making, and early access to community-based care. Within the hospital, clinicians can preserve autonomy by offering choices, revisiting capacity as the patient’s condition changes, inviting trusted supporters into the process (with patient permission), and involving the patient in treatment and discharge planning.

Involuntary hospitalization should not erase a person’s voice and autonomy. Even when patient freedom must be temporarily restricted, dignity, participation, and self-determination should remain at the center of care.

item.title: Why Good Writing Could Hurt Your Relationships
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Why Good Writing Could Hurt Your Relationships

Suddenly, trying hard can seem like you're not trying at all.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • Writers now strip out choices they like to avoid sounding like AI slop.
  • Precise and polished writing used to signal care, but now can trigger doubt.
  • Without an explicit AI label, people are trusting; when labeled AI, writers suffer the penalty.
  • We default to belief, but how honest someone seems barely tracks how honest they are.

I spent four minutes staring dead into the eyes of an em dash.

It was sitting in the second paragraph of a different article I was working on, minding its own business, holding open a pause that my sentence really needed. But I stared at it like it was insulting my mother, and then I deleted it before putting it back in. Then I deleted it again and rebuilt the sentence around the lowly comma, which was much worse, and I knew it was worse the whole time I was doing it.

An editor told me a while back that em dashes are one of the ways she “knows” when the writing came from a bot. Looking around the internet these days, I get it. Suddenly em dashes are everywhere! So now every time I reach for one, a second thought slams up against the first: Oh crap, this is going to look like I didn’t write this. So I swap in something duller, and I feel slightly worse about myself, and I carry on with the rest of the day.

I wasted how long thinking about punctuation? I am a frequent writer. I have a Ph.D. I’ve always admired the mighty em dash, and I’ve reveled in its use since about 1989.

And then I learned that the em dash isn’t even the tell anymore. Go figure. The Economist ran a study this summer comparing the leading AI models against human writing and found that most of them now use fewer em dashes than we do. The machines seem to have moved on months ago, but I’m still out here rewriting perfectly good sentences to duck an accusation that has stopped being accurate.

A Flicker

What makes this even weirder is that I’ve caught myself doing the same thing from the other side of the screen. A friend texted me about something complicated happening in my life. It was a really good note. It was warm and specific, the right length, and he brought up something only someone who actually knew me would know. And in the hot two seconds before I felt gratitude, I’ll admit it: something else flickered past.

Did he really write this?

I felt bad about it. I mean, I’ve known this guy for a long time, and he’s always been a what-you-see-is-what-you-get kind of friend. The little flicker of doubt lasted a heartbeat; I shooed it away, and I wrote back honestly with a smile on my face. But I’ve thought about it dozens of times since.

His message triggered the flicker because it was pretty darn good. If he’d sent me sloppy sentences with typos all over them, I’d have believed him instantly and never thought twice about it. Writing with precision and polish used to read as care, but those no longer prove anyone was behind them. The harder someone tries now, the more they might look like someone who didn’t try at all.

article continues after advertisement

You may recognize your own version of this. Did you get a birthday note that was a little too smooth? Or an email from a colleague that hits every note but somehow feels totally hollow? Or did you read your kid’s essay, which is damn good, maybe a little too good?

On the other hand, maybe none of this happened to you. In a study published early in 2026, people read everyday messages and gave their impressions of the sender. The same messages were given different origin stories: written by a human, written by AI, uncertain who wrote it, no information about the source.

People who were told outright that AI generated the message judged the sender harshly, calling them lazy and insincere. People given zero information about the source trusted the sender as fully as people told a human wrote it, and those told a machine might have been involved remained nearly as trusting.

You might expect heavy AI users to be a little more suspicious, but even that turns out not to be true. Unless explicitly labeled, people trust senders’ words because they assume someone labored over them.

Why did I question whether my friend had written that text? Well, I’m in a totally different category than a heavy AI user. I teach an MBA class about keeping our taste and discernment in an algorithmic world, and I’m a keynote speaker on how to find a life raft on the sea of sameness that AI is partially responsible for creating.

Or maybe none of that matters, and it was just that an editor mentioned em dashes to me once, in passing, and that was enough to make me wary of everyone else.

The Default

Timothy Levine from the University of Oklahoma works on a related question: How do people decide whether to believe each other?

His basic answer is that it mostly isn’t a decision at all. We just believe. He calls this the truth-default: when someone tells us something, we presume honesty and carry on, without ever asking whether they truly mean it. Most of what people say is true (most of the time), so presuming honesty is a good strategy. Belief is our default state, so it takes some kind of intrusion to knock us out of it.

article continues after advertisement

I don’t think my friend was lying to me. If a machine did help him find the right words, the sympathy behind them could still be totally real. I was questioning whether anyone had actually been there when the words were typed out, but that’s an odd thing to wonder about someone you know and care about.

Levine introduced a second finding that might explain why I did a double-take at that em dash. People, it turns out, vary enormously in how believable they seem, and an honest demeanor seems to have little to do with honesty itself. How we come across and how we really are are barely correlated.

With a bit of punctuation, I was managing my demeanor, in written form, so that a sentence I’d already typed with my own lanky fingers would still look like mine. Despite bold claims of nearly unerring accuracy, I think that’s what AI detectors do, too: they process how the writing seems and call the result authorship, whether it’s right or wrong.

The Next One Stays

I texted my friend and told him his note meant a lot, which was completely true. I didn’t bring up that flicker of doubt, and I’ve decided it was never really about him anyway.

The truth is, I have always loved a good em dash! It’s a cool little piece of punctuation, the only thing that really lets a sentence stop and breathe and then head off in another direction. And I don’t think it was taken away from me as punishment; I gave it up myself, for several minutes, to avoid being suspected of something I had not done.

And, well, I lost that one. The comma is still sitting there in a piece I published a few months ago, doing a worse job than the dash would have done, just because I got a little spooked. Now I’ve written this entire piece without using a single one.

So the next one stays—right here, in this sentence, finally doing exactly the job I asked it to do.

item.title: How to Overcome a Creative Block
item.description:
Cognition

How to Overcome a Creative Block

A creative block is a lack of progress, not a lack of ability.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • A creative block is a common experience.
  • The overwhelming emotion behind a creative block is frustration.
  • Cognitive and behavioral regulation strategies help break out of the block.
  • Start with self-compassion, take a break, and examine your problems from different angles
Creative block is not a symptom of a lack of ability
Source: Nick Fewings/Unsplash

Staring at a blank screen or canvass? Ideas simply not coming out? Your mind seems as blank as the surface in front of you? You're likely dealing with a creative block. Psychologists define a creative block as a lack of progress that cannot be explained by a lack of capacity for creativity.

If lack of ability isn’t the issue, what is? A creative block is about the nature of the creative process. When our goal is creativity, we are attempting to do something that hasn’t been done before. Because of this, there is no blueprint to specify what we are doing at every step of the way. Chances are, some degree of trial and error will be necessary, and those errors end up being times of block or impasse.

Another reason for a creative block is failing to see the forest for the trees. This can happen when we get fixated in our thinking. Researchers have found that when we are presented with examples of potential solutions when starting to work on a project, it becomes difficult to detach from them. People end up coming back to examples they see, even if these examples are clearly not what they are looking for. In other words, we might get stuck because we are very deep into one way of thinking at a point that calls for something different.

Although there is no single fail-safe way to get unstuck from a creative block, a number of strategies can help and can be used in combination.

Practice self-compassion

A creative block is a highly emotional experience. When I studied how creative professionals – writers of fiction and nonfiction, composers, painters, sculptors, and designers – describe it, one dominant feeling emerged: frustration. For some, it could be tinged with anger, for others with anxiety, and others still with disappointment or doubt.

A good place to start is by working to dull these feelings. Our goal is not necessarily to transform overwhelming frustration into calm or happiness; that might be too tall an order to achieve immediately. But we can ease the frustration just enough so that it releases its grip.

One strategy is to ask ourselves what we would say to a dear friend who shared a similar experience. Our inner voice can be harsh and self-accusatory, but we are unlikely to speak in such a way to someone else.

Self-compassion means saying the words meant to help others to ourselves. Research shows that this is especially helpful for highly self-critical people. Darya Zabelina and Michael Robinson found that when those who tend to be hard on themselves deliberately focused on self-compassion, they came up with ideas as original as those who were not overly self-critical.

Take a break

Being stuck is like facing a tall wall. And continuing to work for hours or even days without progress is like hitting your head against that wall. Taking a break and walking away from the wall might help us see a new perspective (perhaps we can walk around it?).

Researchers at Lancaster University found that taking a break can improve creative thinking. However, it also matters what we do in this break. Most effective breaks aren’t passive, like watching TV or getting a snack. To be helpful, what we do should require some effort, while also not being too demanding. Responding to email or completing paperwork might do the trick. These activities insert a break from the task on which we are blocked while occupying our mind and letting it disconnect from thinking about the problem.

Allow your mind to wander

Taking a break and switching what we are doing for a short time will often help us break through a bottleneck. But not always.

Experiencing a creative block builds pressure to resume productive work. It can be difficult to give yourself permission to let your mind wander off task. Yet, that can help.

Psychologists studied the work process of two groups of people who are creative in very different ways – writers and theoretical physicists. They found that at any given time, both of these groups were making steady progress. However, in 14% of times, they experienced a creative block.

Although people came up with most of their ideas when they were absorbed in work, about one in five times they got creative ideas when their mind wandered off task. Ideas generated when people were not actively focused on the problem felt like "aha" moments of sudden insight. Importantly, these ideas were similar in quality to ideas produced in times of focus and consistent progress. Letting the mind wander allowed it to stumble onto a new path.

Back to the drawing board

When the first line strategies fail, it is time to reconsider the nature of the problem at hand. Not making progress can be a signal that the way we defined the problem and the road to its solution aren’t working. Perhaps the structure of the story you are writing cannot be saved and needs a rethink. Or the ad design doesn’t satisfy the client and the designers have to identify why and find a different way of approaching the problem. At these times, we need to ask new questions before proceeding with a particular idea.

The truth about the creative block is that there is no single strategy that will help every time. Anything we can do to take the emotional edge off is likely to get us on the right track to open our minds and broaden thinking again. Reaching out to people in our network can allow us to see new perspectives. Because they have not been thinking and working on the problem intensely, they might be able to see it in a different light and provide or inspire a new way for us to approach it. And sometimes getting stuck can mean we have reached an end of one road.

item.title: Searching for Balance in the AI Arms Race
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Searching for Balance in the AI Arms Race

Managing the rapid pace of AI development in daily life.

Posted September 28, 2026

Four years ago, if you had told me that I would be adding language to my syllabus regarding students’ use of AI, I would not have believed you. At the time, I probably did not fully understand the direction AI was going in nor how it was rapidly starting to revolutionize how students learn and how I teach psychology courses.

I recently created an online asynchronous course and I received substantial feedback on how to “AI-proof assignments” in light of the crafty ways some students may use AI to bypass the intellectual rigor of course assignments. In that course, instead of students simply writing and submitting a paper (which is vulnerable to uses of AI), they must complete the paper in several different parts, requiring them to demonstrate their learning process. Ensuring that students are appropriately challenged in the era of generative AI has become my second full-time job.

As a psychology professor and licensed psychologist, what’s even more concerning is the risk of “cognitive stunting.” When young people, who are still learning how to master certain skills (e.g., summarizing text), decide to “outsource” these skills to AI, they are “shortcutting the process of developing those skills in the first place,” explains Rebecca Winthrop in a piece published by the Brookings Institute. The concerns are even greater for children and adolescents. They simply do not possess the cognitive reserve to offload these cognitive tasks, so the skill never gets developed.

Now, we’re facing an uncanny set of events with the proliferation of generative AI in all facets of life, which is being met with a mixture of pushback, acceptance, skepticism, and wonder. New York City Mayor Mamdani announced a one-year ban on generative AI in all New York City public schools. Los Angeles Unified School District (LAUSD) banned generative AI as well.

On the other hand, Alpha School, an AI-driven, teacher free school, launched its newest location in Chicago, Illinois in September 2026. A few months ago, a rural, upstate New York school paused the deployment of a human-like AI powered robot, following backlash. Where I work, at the University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB), undergraduates can pursue a Bachelor of Science in Artificial Intelligence, which prepares students to design AI systems responsibly based on real world data.

The sudden ubiquity of AI is fascinating, unexpected, and perhaps disconcerting, particularly when we remind ourselves that OpenAI released ChatGPT in November 2022. That means that generative AI has only been available for public use for less than 5 years. This rate of accelerated development seems implausible yet so many of us are being inundated with notifications about companies’ adoption of AI tools. Gmail has Gemini as a built-in AI email assistant; Meta recently released Muse, a personal AI assistant; Amazon has Alexa to help with online shopping; and Bank of America has Erica, a virtual financial assistant.

The emergence of new technology is fun, exciting, but sometimes it provokes resistance. For example, books have been around for thousands of years with clay tablets and papyrus rolls being cited as the earliest known books since the third millennium BC. Socrates, the Ancient Greek Philosopher, decried the use of books arguing that it diluted human intelligence, by relying on the written word instead of memory. Furthermore, a book couldn’t challenge a reader the way a skilled instructor could when teaching students.

Consider even more recent technology such as the calculator. In the 1970s, the first handheld calculator was introduced to the public and was immediately popular. Resistance and concern followed thereafter. In 1986, teachers protested along the streets of a Washington D.C. convention center where the National Council of Teachers of Mathematics (NCTM) had convened a meeting. They protested the NCTM’s new policy that calculators be integrated into K-12 education. They carried signs passionately saying, “The Button's Nothin' ‘til the Brain's Trained.” Teachers feared that calculators would interfere with natural human intelligence and argued that pervasive use of the calculator would prevent students from acquiring the important skills needed to solve fundamental math operations.

In light of these mixed directions, where do we go from here? On one hand, generative AI can impact necessary, real-world experiences that make us human such as:

  • Making mistakes
  • Being creative
  • Taking risks
  • Pursuing social and romantic relationships
  • Experiencing hardships

This can lead people to being:

  • Less social
  • Less confident
  • Less emotionally regulated

There are probably a handful more reasons why generative AI can be harmful to older and developing minds alike. However, the unstoppable, lightning speed development of generative AI places us in a quandary when trying to determine the most proactive, reasonable way to deal with it.

Given that generative AI appears to be here to stay, understanding how to use this tool responsibly seems, in my view, to be the best way to inoculate ourselves against its potentially damaging effects. Some studies have suggests that when AI is used in specific, targeted ways among teachers, it may actually promote problem solving and critical thinking in students. Use of generative AI can, in some cases, save time, cut costs, or increase productivity, amongst other things. With that said, it will be helpful to prepare people on how to use AI responsibly.

  • Age minimums. For example, users must often be at least 13 years old and have parental consent before creating an account to use certain generative AI tools (although an important caveat here is that many can still be used without creating an account).
  • Establishing parameters for use. AI has been shown to be helpful in explaining complex, technical tasks. So, in the context of parents helping their children with homework, AI could provide step by step guidance on how to solve linear equations or geometry proofs, for example. This sort of guidance could serve as a template for other math problems.
  • Transparency in AI use. Disclosing use of AI is responsible. The editor of Winthrop’s Brooking’s commentary disclosed use of AI for light copyediting and search for sources. Whenever possible, this sort of disclosure should become more mainstream.

As our understanding of generative AI continues to grow, we should continue to be mindful of its impact on how we complete mundane and complex tasks. Rather than barring its use, I believe that figuring out how to use it responsibly should be what guides us through these uncharted waters.

item.title: New Kitten Guardians Should Ask These Questions
item.description:
Animal Behavior

New Kitten Guardians Should Ask These Questions

When getting kittens, let the good times roll for future behavioral health.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • It's best to get two kittens if you can, rather than one.
  • For kittens, a range of good early life experiences is important for their development.
  • Kittens who meet multiple people when very young grow up to be friendlier to people and less afraid.

If you’re getting a kitten or two, it pays to ask questions about the kitten’s early life at the breeder, rescue, or shelter. That’s because an excellent start to life can make a big difference to their behavioral development and therefore to their life with you.

Kittens have what’s known as a sensitive period for socialization between the ages of about 2 and 7-9 weeks. This is a time when their brain is developing rapidly. Having a wide range of positive experiences can help them grow up into friendly, confident adult cats. But since kittens don’t go to their new home until they are at least 8 weeks old (and later seems to be better), it’s important to find out about your potential kitten’s early life experiences.

Play is important for kitten development
Source: Michelle-Maria/Pixabay

Whoever is raising the kittens in those early weeks should be taking care to give the kitten lots of experience with the people, animals, and things they might meet later in life. Interactions with new people at this early age are important for helping your kitten to learn to be sociable around people. So check that the kitten is meeting human visitors and also other animals. The effects are long-lasting. Kittens who are well socialized at this age spend more time close to people when they are a year old and will more easily learn to trust a new person (Casey and Bradshaw, 2008; Turner, 2021).

It’s not just about people. Ensure that the kittens are being raised in a household environment, rather than a shed in the garden, for example, so that they are being exposed to normal household sounds. Shelters and rescues often send kittens to foster homes, but even when they are having to raise kittens in a shelter environment, they should be taking steps to get the kittens used to things like the sound of a washing machine.

Meet the kittens’ mom and check that she is friendly to other people too. If it’s possible to meet the father, which is quite likely for pedigree kittens but not so much at a shelter/rescue, check that they are friendly and sociable as well. Health is also very important, and you want to ensure that the mom and kittens are in good health. Since stress can affect health (and behavioral health), you also want to make sure they are in a relaxed environment.

You might notice at the top that I said a kitten “or two”. That’s because having another kitten around can be very beneficial. Kitten play peaks in those early weeks when they are in their new home (up until about 14 weeks), and the kittens will spend a lot of time playing together. Play isn’t just fun; it’s also important from a developmental perspective. The kittens are practicing things like motor control, predatory behaviors, and social skills. Plus, if you want more than one cat, getting them as a bonded pair of kittens avoids the issues that might arise if you later add an unrelated cat to your household.

Once the kitten(s) come to you, you can build on their early experiences and help ensure they keep on having more positive experiences. Always give your kitten(s) a choice of whether or not to interact with people and objects. Kittens are so tiny and cute that people often subject them to handling whether or not they like it; but pay attention to their body language for signs that they might be uncomfortable and don’t force handling on them.

This is a good time to get them used to handling that they will experience later in life, such as brushing, toothbrushing, having their paws handled for nail trims, and so on. But always keep sessions short and break things down into sections that are not just manageable but actually fun for the kitten. For example, don’t just launch into brushing your kitten’s teeth, but take time to get them used to the toothbrush, pet toothpaste, and the handling separately before you start to put them together. Use treats, play, and petting to make it a positive experience. Never force your kitten to do things because that risks making them fearful. Bad experiences in early life can have a long-lasting effect, so work hard to make things relaxed, pleasant, and fun.

If there is a kitten kindergarten class near you, this is a good opportunity for you and the kitten to learn. While these classes are increasing in popularity, they can still be hard to find. Even if there isn’t such a class near you, take some time to learn more about kitten and cat behavior from a reliable source. Doing so will help you to understand your cat better, become able to provide for their needs, and help to ensure a happy relationship with your cat over the years.

item.title: How to Be Inspired by Autumn
item.description:
Gratitude

How to Be Inspired by Autumn

Autumn teaches us to embrace change, let go gently, and savor what is here now.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • Autumn trees remind us that letting go takes time.
  • Letting go can be less dramatic than we imagine or fear.
  • Enjoy what is here while it's here.
  • We can appreciate what a season gives us while trusting ourselves to find a way to what comes next.

I expect all of us who love summer’s long, sunny days hate to see them wind down. Cool mornings take until afternoon to warm up. The light quilt on the bed seems to portend the down comforter that will follow as autumn moves toward winter.

But autumn brings pleasures of its own. Here in Atlanta, the cooler air is a welcome relief after 76 days at or above 90 degrees this summer. We’ll likely have warm weather well into October, and the trees may wait until late in the month or early November to begin their annual transformation.

Still, something has shifted. The morning air feels different against my skin—cool, even chilly. The light falls at a gentler angle. I find myself lingering outside instead of hurrying toward the air-conditioned indoors.

Autumn Invites Us to Notice Change While It's Happening

Most of us are better at recognizing change afterward. We look back and see that a friendship deepened (or disappeared), a difficult year made us more resourceful, or a familiar way of living no longer fit. While we’re in the middle of it, though, change can feel uncertain. Even a welcome transition may involve giving up something, someone, or some place, we love.

Autumn beckons us to think in new ways about change.
Source: John-ManuelAndriote/photo

I can be grateful for cooler weather and still miss a summer evening that seemed to go on forever. Both feelings can be true. Autumn reminds me that accepting the next season doesn’t require me to disown the last one. I have been grateful for a warm, humid night in July. And I have also been grateful for crisp bright October afternoons. Gratitude is the common denominator.

The trees offer another lesson: Letting go takes time. A leaf doesn’t turn brilliant red one morning and fall that afternoon. Its color changes gradually. For a while, green and gold share the same branch. Eventually the tree releases what it has spent months growing.

We often expect ourselves to move faster than that. We think we should be over a disappointment, ready for a new relationship, or certain about our next chapter by now. But a meaningful change may need its own season. Sometimes we have to live with mixed feelings for a while before we know what we’re ready to release.

Reading my journals for the book I plan to write about male caregivers, I’m reminded of how long I raged against my circumstances—feeling stuck in my old hometown with no work opportunities after my plan to open a coffeehouse in the struggling downtown didn’t get off the ground. I understand now that the season wasn’t ripe for much-needed change because first I was needed to be my late mom’s caregiver, thereby fulfilling my lifelong prayer somehow to care for Mom in her old age

article continues after advertisement

Letting go can also be less dramatic than we imagine. It may mean no longer rehearsing an old argument every time we’re alone in the car. It may mean retiring an expectation of ourselves that once made sense but now leaves us exhausted. Or it may mean accepting that someone we care about cannot give us the relationship we hoped for. None of these decisions happens once and for all. We may need to make them again on many ordinary mornings.

Autumn Also Asks What We Want to Carry Forward

As the year begins to narrow, I’m tempted to measure it by what I haven’t done. The unfinished project and the goal that slipped away can crowd out everything else. A walk or a hike on a mild October afternoon can interrupt that accounting. It gives me room to remember a conversation that mattered, work I’m proud of, or simply to enjoy the beauty of the autumn leaves. And there is ample beauty in the fall when, as Thoreau described it, the entire forest can seem a garden of brightly colored blossoms if we pay attention and see it through our imagination.

That kind of attention is an act of resilience. When life has been hard, it can feel safer to focus on what went wrong so we won’t be caught off guard again. Yet noticing what sustained us helps us recognize what we can rely on: a friend who called, a routine that steadied us, our own capacity to keep going.

As the days shorten, we might also give ourselves permission to slow down. Summer’s long daylight can create the illusion that we should always be out doing more. Autumn offers a different rhythm: an earlier evening at home, a meal shared with a friend, a book opened under a lamp. Rest doesn’t have to be earned by exhaustion. It can be part of living well.

Soon enough, Atlanta’s trees will put on their fall show. Some leaves will blaze for weeks; others will turn and disappear before I think to look up. I want to pay attention this year. I want to enjoy what is here while it is here, including the last warm afternoons, without asking them to last.

Perhaps that is autumn’s most useful inspiration. We cannot make a season stay. We can meet it with curiosity, appreciate what it gives us, and trust ourselves to find a way into what comes next.

item.title: Why I Became a Student Again in My 40s
item.description:
Education

Why I Became a Student Again in My 40s

Personal Perspective: There are flashcards on my nightstand like it's 2004.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • Adults learn differently, and the study habits that feel productive are often the least effective.
  • Testing yourself, taking real breaks, and studying with others beat rereading and cramming.
  • Being willing to be a beginner again is one of the most underrated sources of growth and joy.

After 14 years as an attending anesthesiologist, I voluntarily signed up to sit in a testing center, silence my phone, and take another board exam. This time it's in obesity medicine. My friends think I've lost it. My husband has learned not to ask why the kitchen table is covered in highlighters and sticky tabs.

Here's what nobody tells you about reinvention. From the outside, it looks glamorous. From the inside, it looks like a middle-aged woman at a desk at 9 p.m., furiously scribbling notes about hormones and hunger signaling.

And yet, I'm loving it.

Why Go Back to School Now?

Obesity affects roughly 40 percent of adults in the United States, and it remains one of the most misunderstood, most stigmatized, and most undertreated conditions I see. When I went to medical school, we barely touched nutrition. GLP-1 medications weren't part of the conversation. Longevity was something you read about in magazines, not in textbooks.

Now my patients ask me about all of it. And I don't want to help them with a hot take. I want to help them with the evidence. So I study.

What surprised me most is how different learning feels this time around. In my 20s, I memorized to survive. I studied because the next exam was coming, and failure was not an option. Now I study because I'm genuinely curious, and because the knowledge has somewhere to go the moment I learn it.

Adults Learn Differently (and That's a Good Thing)

Educator Malcolm Knowles, who popularized the concept of andragogy, or adult learning theory, argued that adults learn best when the material is relevant to their lives, when they have some control over how they learn, and when they can connect new information to experience they already have.

That tracks. At 20, a fact about metabolism was just a fact. At 42, it's the patient I saw last week, the conversation I had with a friend over dinner, and the question someone asked me on Instagram. Every new piece of information has a hook to hang on. That's not a disadvantage of learning later in life. It's the advantage.

The catch is that most of us are still using the study habits we built as teenagers, and a lot of those habits don't hold up.

What the Science Says About Studying (That I Wish I'd Known at 20)

1. Test yourself instead of rereading. Rereading your notes feels productive because the material starts to look familiar. But familiar isn't the same as learned. In a well-known study, psychologists Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke found that students who practiced recalling information remembered significantly more a week later than students who simply restudied it. This is called the testing effect, and it's why my flashcards live on my nightstand.

article continues after advertisement

2. Take real breaks. I use a modified Pomodoro method: 50 minutes heads-down, then 10 minutes up. I stretch, play with the dog, grab a snack, and sometimes bang out a set of high knees or jumping jacks (because you have to walk the walk if you're going to talk the talk). Then I sit back down. Breaks aren't a reward for studying. They're part of studying. And sleep is where a lot of the memory consolidation happens, which is my favorite scientific excuse to be in bed by 9:30 (remember on The Real Housewives of Dallas when I had a party but asked everyone to leave at a reasonable time? Yeah—sorry not sorry).

3. Don't do it alone. One of my friends is sitting for the same exam, and we decided that if we were going to do this, we weren't going to do it halfway. We met up in San Diego for a study-and-spa weekend. We quizzed each other. We ate healthy snacks. We worked out. We hiked (one mile, but that counts). Then we capped it off with a three-Michelin-star dinner, including Wagyu from cows that apparently only eat olives. (Who knew that was a thing?) Was it the most extra way imaginable to cram for a medical board? Absolutely. But having a study buddy made the whole thing feel less like a grind and more like an adventure.

The Hardest Part Isn't the Material

Here's the part I didn't expect. The hardest part of going back to school wasn't learning the content. It was being a beginner again.

High achievers are used to being the one with the answers. We've spent years building expertise, and our identity is often tied to being competent. So when you sit down with a practice question and get it wrong, it doesn't just feel like a wrong answer. It feels like a small threat to who you are.

Psychologist Carol Dweck's research on growth mindset shows that people who view their abilities as something they can develop, rather than something fixed, are more likely to embrace challenges and persist through setbacks. I've had to practice this in real time. Every wrong answer on a practice exam is information, not a verdict. I'm not bad at this. I'm new at this. Those are very different things.

Learning as a Source of Joy

I write a lot about joy, and I'll be honest, I didn't expect a board exam to be one of my sources of it this year. But there's something deeply energizing about being curious again — about reading something and thinking, "Wait, really?" and about realizing that after two decades in medicine, there is so much I still don't know, and I get to go find out.

article continues after advertisement

So here's my prescription for you. Pick one thing you've been curious about and give yourself permission to be bad at it for a while. Take the class. Learn the language. Sign up for the certification you keep talking yourself out of. You don't need a board exam to justify it.

You are never too accomplished, too busy, or too "done" to be a beginner again. In fact, the willingness to learn something new might be the whole secret to reinvention.

Now if you'll excuse me, my flashcards are waiting.

item.title: Why More Women Are Keeping Their Names After Marriage
item.description:
Marriage

Why More Women Are Keeping Their Names After Marriage

Signs suggest more women in the U.S. are choosing to keep their birth name when they get married.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • Around the world, millions of married women keep their birth name for life, even after having children.
  • U.S. women are outpacing men in masters, doctorates, and professional degrees, and marrying later in life.
  • The more education a woman obtains, the more likely she keeps her birth name after marriage.
  • Until U.S. courts halted required name changes in the 1960s and 70s, wives had to change their name to drive.

I heard “Congratulations to the future Mrs. Kelce” on the radio this spring.

Despite being among the most famous and successful women in the world and holding a larger net worth than her now husband, Travis Kelce, even Taylor Swift experienced the social presumptions of taking her husband’s last name after marriage. Why? And will young Swifties, and other unwed women, encounter the same “traditional” naming pressures if they decide to marry in the future?

Only time will tell, but some signs suggest more young women may be choosing to keep their birth name rather than automatically taking their husband’s last name.

In the U.S., Women Often Take a Husband’s Last Name

For background, approximately 79 percent of U.S. women change their last name to their husbands, according to a 2023 Pew Research study. Many of these women are motivated by their desire to have children and/or prioritize a unified family name.

Women changing their names is also common in counties like the United Kingdom, Australia, Japan, and parts of Canada.

Source: Jeyaratnam Caniceus from Pixabay

Globally, Women Commonly Keep Their Birth Name

However, millions of women throughout the world do not change their name after marriage, or even after having children. In countries like Spain, Chile, and Mexico, women traditionally keep their birth surnames for life, as do women in China, South Korea, and Vietnam. In many African societies, women protect their lineage by keeping their birth names.

In Greece, it’s illegal for a woman to formally take her husband’s surname after marriage. Quebec has a similar law. In other countries, like France and Italy, some women may socially adjust their name to have a “family” name, but a woman does not legally change from her birth name.

The bottom line is that every day, millions of couples around the globe raise children and stay married, despite different last names—and younger American women are likely more exposed to this global perspective than they were in the past.

Why the Different Naming Tradition In the U.S.?

During America’s colonial period, English settlers brought to the U.S. “coverture” (English common law). Among other things, it meant that when a father “gave away the bride," it was literal. The woman changed her birth name to her husband’s last name. Then, the husband held all his wife’s legal rights—to keep wages, own property, maintain custody of their children etc., (remember, the U.S. Constitution only granted women the right to vote in 1920).

This coverture lasted in various forms until as recently as the 1960s and 70s, when courts started striking down forced name changes. In 1966, former U.S. Supreme Court Justice Hugo Black wrote in United States v. Yazell, that coverture...

“...rests on the old common-law fiction that the husband and wife are one… This rule has worked out in reality to mean that though the husband and wife are one, the one is the husband.”

In another ruling, Dunn v. Palermo, in 1975 the Tennessee Supreme Court struck down a law requiring women to take their husband’s name to vote or get a driver’s license. And 51 years later, some official forms continue to be updated, asking for “birth” name rather than the outdated “maiden” term.

Knowing this history, it is easier to understand how for a long time, many women stayed married simply because it was not legally, financially, or socially possible to leave.

The Belief In Needing to Share a Last Name is Shifting

Thanks, in-part, to court rulings, today, women are making more of their own name choices.

The same 2023 Pew Research study also found that approximately 14 percent of all women in an opposite sex marriage opt to keep their last name. Yet of the younger women (18-49), approximately 20 percent kept their birth names after marriage, compared to 9 percent of women 50+, suggesting a name preference shift is already happening.

Among unmarried women, the study found only 33 percent said that they would take their husband’s last name. Another 17 percent opted to hyphenate both names.

In another shift, a 2025 YouGov poll found that more than half of U.S. citizens do not believe a married couple needs to share a last name to reflect commitment.

Source: s1601064 from Pixabay

The More Educated, the More Likely She Will Keep Her Birth Name

Younger women are also opting more for college and to marry later. Since 1965, the median age when a woman marries has gone from 20.6 to 28.4 in 2025.

As we look at education rates today, women are now earning nearly twice as many master’s degrees as men, 40 percent more doctoral degrees, and women far outnumber men in professional programs. Women are also increasingly earning as much or more money than their husbands.

Education numbers are worth noting because college-educated women marry at higher rates than women who didn’t attend college. Furthermore, nearly one-third of married women with a postgraduate degree keep or hyphenate their name.

Considering all this, as we look to the future, it’s worth asking:

  • Will more educated women self-sacrifice or risk professional setbacks by changing their identity later in life?
  • Will women who seek a marriage of equals just “Shake it off” when only 2 percent of men say that they would take a woman’s last name?
  • Will younger women find changing their name worth it when a May 2025 YouGov survey found that 42 percent of men think women should change their name back after a divorce?
  • And will educated women even acknowledge anyone who misconstrues correlation with causation, and suggests a couple ends up divorced because the woman did not take the man’s last name ten years earlier? (Divorce is expensive and high-income women—who are more likely to keep their birth name—are more likely to have the financial resources to leave an unhealthy marriage sooner.)

The “End Game”

“Mrs.” comments, like the one I heard on the radio, are usually said with good intentions, without thinking. But in 2026, aren't these women telling us that we should pause to think before we assume a woman must change the legal identity she’s held since birth because she got married?

Times do change and marriages and societies do adapt—even when changing traditions is hard.

Ultimately, healthy marriages benefit families and communities. Much like the people in countries across the globe who accept a bride’s birth name, maybe younger women are teaching us that we should be supportive of any name chosen by a married woman—including Taylor Swift.

item.title: When Being Too Understanding Hurts You
item.description:
Relationships

When Being Too Understanding Hurts You

Understanding someone’s behavior doesn’t erase the harm it causes.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • Understanding why someone hurt you doesn’t erase that they hurt you.
  • Empathy and accountability can exist at the same time.
  • Self-reflection becomes harmful when it causes you to distrust your own experience.
  • You can understand someone’s pain without taking responsibility for their behavior.
Source: Odonata Wellnesscenter/ Pexels

Daniel’s father was furious with him for not inviting his latest girlfriend. Daniel had met several girlfriends over the years, many of whom had disappeared almost as quickly as they appeared. After getting to know these girlfriends only to have to say goodbye shortly after, he decided he didn’t want to keep getting involved. He told his father he’d meet a new girlfriend only after the relationship lasted at least six months.

His father didn’t take it well. He called Daniel selfish, complained to other family members behind his back, and announced he wouldn’t go back to Daniel’s house without the girlfriend.

Daniel was hurt and angry by his father’s reaction. However, almost immediately, he started explaining his father’s behavior to himself.

My dad was abandoned as a child. He’s always been sensitive to rejection. Maybe this felt like another rejection. Was six months too harsh? I could have just let him bring her over. What’s the harm? Maybe supporting him means supporting his relationships too.

Quickly, Daniel wasn’t thinking much about how his father’s response affected him. He was building a case for why his father had responded that way, and slowly talking himself out of his own feelings.

I know I have done this myself. Have you? Understanding why someone hurt you doesn’t require you to explain away the hurt they have caused.

Psychology helps us understand why people behave the way they do. We know more about trauma, attachment, family dynamics, emotional regulation, and mental health. This understanding creates compassion. But sometimes, especially for people who are naturally empathetic or psychologically minded, understanding becomes a way to rationalize ourselves out of our own experiences and hurt.

She had a difficult childhood.

He was never taught how to communicate.

She’s going through a terrible time.

He has abandonment issues.

All of these may be true, but sometimes, “I understand why they did it” can become “therefore, I shouldn’t be hurt by it.”

Those are two different things.

A person's history may explain their behavior without making the behavior acceptable. Their pain may help us understand their reaction, but it shouldn’t erase its natural consequences.

Are You Talking Yourself Out of Your Feelings?

I don’t think the answer is to stop questioning ourselves. From a Bowen family systems perspective, being willing to examine ourselves is an important part of differentiation. We can ask ourselves: Was I unnecessarily harsh? Did I contribute to this problem? Is my position thoughtful, or am I reacting emotionally, too?

Daniel can ask himself these questions. Self-examination is healthy, though self-examination can turn into self-erasure when every explanation for another person’s behavior becomes another reason to distrust our own experience and pain.

Daniel can also ask: Even if my father felt rejected, was it okay for him to insult me to other family members? Does understanding his sensitivity mean I have to reverse my decision? Can my father be genuinely hurt and still be responsible for what he does with that hurt?

The goal is to see the whole picture without erasing anyone’s experience or the consequences of their actions. People often behave badly when they’re hurting—this is understandable.

Someone who has experienced abandonment may become highly reactive to rejection. Someone raised around anger might learn to respond to conflict with anger. Someone who grew up in an emotionally volatile family may struggle to regulate themselves when relationships feel uncertain.

But people with similar experiences don’t always respond in the same ways. Our histories influence us. They don’t necessarily dictate every choice we make. This is where empathy and accountability can coexist.

These statements can coexist: I understand why this is especially painful for you. And: The way you handled that pain hurt me.

We don’t have to choose between compassion and reality. Bowen family systems theory encourages us to look beyond individual behavior and observe the emotional process occurring between people.

In Daniel’s relationship, the pattern might look like this:

His father feels rejected and becomes angry. Daniel becomes anxious and guilty. He begins explaining his father’s behavior to himself. Then Daniel questions his own position and considers giving in. If he does, his father’s anxiety decreases, and the relationship returns to normal. Daniel’s job isn’t to diagnose his father or convince him that his behavior is wrong. It’s to become more aware of his part in the pattern.

Does he repeatedly give in because he has thoughtfully changed his mind, or because his father’s anger is difficult for him to tolerate?

That’s an important distinction. Systems thinking doesn’t mean everyone is equally responsible for every behavior. Daniel can examine himself without taking responsibility for his father’s insults. His father is responsible for his behavior. Daniel is responsible for what Daniel does next.

Accountability Doesn’t Require Condemnation

Mental illness, trauma, childhood experiences, and emotional limitations can all affect a person’s capacity to respond differently. Those things matter. But reduced capacity doesn’t mean everyone around that person should absorb the consequences.

You can have compassion for someone’s limitations and still recognize what those limitations mean for your relationship with them.

If you notice yourself doing what Daniel does, slow down and ask yourself:

Am I trying to understand this person, or am I trying to make what happened hurt less?

If I didn’t know this person’s history, how would I view the behavior itself?

Can I understand why this person reacted this way and still acknowledge how the reaction affected me?

After stepping back, Daniel may decide that six months was unnecessarily rigid and change his position. Or he may decide that he doesn’t want to keep bringing his father’s short-term relationships into his home. Either decision can be thoughtful.

What matters is that Daniel isn’t making it to relieve the anxiety created by his father’s reaction. He can eventually arrive at a position that holds more than one truth:

I understand why this hurt my dad. Knowing his history helps me be compassionate. I can also recognize that insulting me and involving other family members wasn’t okay.

That’s what healthy empathy actually asks of us. Not to explain away behavior. Certainly not to deny another person’s suffering, and not to deny our own. Empathy doesn’t require us to make harmful behavior harmless. We can understand where someone came from, recognize the pain they hold, and still be honest about the pain they caused.
