item.title: Why You Need to Sit Up Straight
item.description:
Body Language

Why You Need to Sit Up Straight

Update on one of the most-watched TED Talks — and one of the most contested.

Posted September 28, 2026

In 2010, Amy Cuddy and two other authors published a research study that suggested that if you stood confidently, with your hands on your hips like Wonder Woman, you would actually transform your mental state by increasing testosterone and decreasing cortisol. Her TED talk of 2012, “Your Body Language May Shape Who You Are,” which has gained more than 77 million views so far, took the idea a little further, saying that while body language indicates to other people how we feel, specifically how powerful we seem, our own body language also suggests to ourselves how powerful we are. She asked the question, could you fake it until you make it? And the talk concludes with a touching story about, as Amy says, “faking it until you become it.”

That initial widespread notice brought about a reaction — other researchers failed to find the same result in terms of hormonal changes. Everyone did agree, however, that if standing confidently made you feel more confident, there was nothing wrong with “faking it until you made it — or became it.”

Recently, a new study published in the British Journal of Psychology cleverly avoids the issues with the original Cuddy et al. study and offers insight into how our bodies affect our minds — and why we should care about that.

Some 200 subjects were instructed to play a risk-taking game on a tablet. The tablet was positioned so that some of the subjects had to sit up straight to play the game and some had to slouch. None of them knew that they were being tested on their body language. The results were striking. The subjects that slouched felt less enthusiastic and took less effective risks — they performed more poorly — than the subjects taking an upright posture. The research subjects with upright postures engaged in more successful play, taking more effective risks.

In the 19th century, the great psychologist William James suggested a similar idea. We smile when we are happy — as a result of that happiness, he noted — but if we push ourselves to smile when we are not happy, that act itself will cause us to feel happier. Experienced performers know this, developing individual rituals to get themselves into enough of a high-energy state to deliver a great performance, whether it’s listening to upbeat music (and dancing to it), bouncing on a trampoline, or fist-pumping backstage to embrace the energy.

The physical state reflects our mental state — and the reverse is also true. You can, and should, use this insight to elevate your presence when preparing for an important presentation, meeting, or negotiation.

Recently, I was coaching a leader getting ready for a high-stakes presentation to his board. He knew his speech cold; he had practiced the delivery so that it sounded confident and assured. He had thought about his goals for the presentation with the audience in front of him. But in what would have been the final rehearsal, I noticed that he had a slight stoop in his posture. His shoulders were slightly rounded, and as a result, he wasn’t taking up his full height. I coached him to stand up straight, sounding a little like my grandmother instructing me many years ago as a boy, and immediately several things happened. He was able to enter the room more confidently, and his voice had more energy in it. But most importantly, he reported that he felt more confident. His body language was instructing him, and thus would also signal confidence and authority to his audience when the moment came.

When you get your moment on the stage, make sure that you are standing as tall as you can, taking up all the space with all the confidence you are entitled to. That little shift in body language will win with your audience — and with you.

item.title: How to Become a Leader at Work Without Even Trying
item.description:
Leadership

How to Become a Leader at Work Without Even Trying

The typical path to leadership often looks similar regardless of industry.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • Leaders often emerge by stepping up for meaningful work, not by chasing titles or rewards.
  • Servant leadership—putting the mission and team first—leads to lasting respect and success.
  • Promotion based on similarity or seniority often overlooks vital skills for leadership roles.

I’ve worked with many leaders and am always looking for patterns. I’ve noticed something common among the most productive and respected leaders I’ve met: their rise to leadership seemed to follow a similar path, despite being in different industries and organizations.

How the Most Effective Leaders Begin Their Journey

The leaders I’m thinking of did not start their careers with the goal of becoming a leader. Instead, they had a passion for the work they were doing, and a willingness to step up when something needed to be done.

That first step in their eventual leadership journey might have been accepting an invitation to a committee, or agreeing to lead a new project, or willingness to add a role to their duties. Of course these individuals were probably approached for these opportunities because they had already shown indications that they are reliable, productive, and agreeable to work with.

That first step often led to meeting new people and gaining broader recognition for their good work. So, these individuals were subsequently more likely to be approached when other needs arose. Typically, their motive for accepting these new roles and tasks was not about “what’s in it for me?” Indeed, most of the time these opportunities required extra effort without compensation, and perhaps not even much expressed recognition or appreciation. The common motive seemed to be “This is something worthwhile that needs to be done, no one else is doing it, and so I’m willing to give it my best shot.”

The Role of Servant Leadership in Sustainable Success

What these rising leaders typically demonstrated were the principles of servant leadership. They stepped in to do what was necessary to advance the mission of the team or organization because they saw it as a worthwhile mission. They saw how their effort could contribute to the greater good, and the results would be personally rewarding as a result. The mission was worthy of their effort.

This process, or path, of one opportunity leading to another seemed to describe how many of the best leaders I’ve known rose to the high levels of leadership in which they served by the time I met them. Certainly this isn’t the only path to leadership, but any path that relies on motivation from extrinsic rewards, such as a higher salary or more authority, seems less likely to succeed, especially with regard to personal satisfaction and respect from followers.

The path to leadership that I’ve described seems like a desirable one, both for the individual and the organization, but may not be the most common path to relatively high levels of leadership. The leaders I’m describing may be a select bunch. The reason I met these leaders is because they continued to experience a drive to improve, and to help those they led to improve as well. That’s how and why I ended up working with them.

Unfortunately, it frequently seems as though individuals are chosen for promotion to leadership because those individuals are a lot like the leaders doing the choosing. The candidate for promotion is both likeable and feels like a “safe bet” because of their similarity to the established leader. Of course we can imagine why “is a lot like me” is not the best criterion for selecting leaders.

Another less-than-ideal criterion for selecting leaders is their productivity at the job for which they were hired. This criterion is often combined with the criterion of “seniority” in selecting who to promote to management. In the 1970s there was a popular business book titled “The Peter Principle.” Simply put, the Peter Principle states that in any large, hierarchical organization, employees tend to rise to the level of their incompetence. How does this happen?

The short answer is that the skills and abilities to succeed vary according to the role. As obvious as this is, it seems to be overlooked in many promotion decisions. Someone who is a successful salesperson and has been around the longest commonly gets promoted to manager of salespeople. Management requires a skill set that is at least somewhat different than is required for success in sales. So, if that new manager does not receive adequate professional development, they’re liable to be stuck at that level, functioning below expectations, and frustrating themselves and those they manage.

Suppose that new manager does adapt and, over time, proves themselves to be a successful manager. They may be rewarded with a promotion to a higher-level job involving strategic leadership. However, the skill set required for success as a manager is not necessarily the same skill set required for successful strategic leadership. And so on.

When the Peter Principle is in play, over time the organization suffers. Those employees who rose to management and leadership positions are relatively incompetent and unlikely to find a better job elsewhere, and those employees bothered by working under incompetent management and leadership leave the organization.

Key Takeaways for Aspiring Leaders

What does all of this mean for you? First, when offered a promotion, or the opportunity to apply for one, ask yourself some difficult questions rather than assuming that a promotion is always a good thing. I wrote in more depth about this issue here. Regardless of whether you aspire to leadership, consider what motivates your best work. If your work doesn’t seem to contribute meaningfully to a mission you find worthwhile, consider job crafting – the process of modifying you job duties to be more personally relevant. This may include integrating new tasks or roles that resonate for you. I wrote in more depth about job crafting here.

Last, consider every new step in your career path, no matter how small, as an opportunity to learn and to establish new relationships. This perspective not only makes your current work more fulfilling, it creates unforeseen opportunities down the road. If or when you find yourself in a new role, recognize that the skills and abilities that got you there may not be those that you need to succeed now. Fortunately there are seemingly endless resources available to you for whatever types of professional development you may need.

item.title: Why Love Languages are Important—and Matching is Essential
item.description:
Relationships

Why Love Languages are Important—and Matching is Essential

How Chapman’s five love languages really impact relationship satisfaction.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • Partners have five preferences for expressing and receiving romantic feelings called love languages.
  • Those five preferences are quality time, physical touch, words of affirmation, acts of service, and gifts.
  • Languages differ in popularity and in importance for relationship satisfaction and sexual fulfillment.
  • Nevertheless, partners who match each other’s love language preferences are more satisfied overall.

In his book, The Five Love Languages, Chapman (1992) relates his clinical observations about how relationship partners share their feelings of attraction, love, and commitment. He also identifies five love languages commonly used by couples to communicate and help each other feel most loved. Those languages are:

  • Physically Touching each other by hugging, kissing, holding hands, or through other expressions of physical intimacy.
  • Spending Quality Time together, especially while having meaningful conversations and engaging in enjoyable activities.
  • Sharing Words of Affirmation with each other, like compliments, expressions of gratitude, and supportive comments.
  • Providing Acts of Service by doing things like helping each other, finishing chores, running errands, and cleaning up.
  • Giving Gifts to each other to mark special occasions, be thoughtful, or spontaneously show affection.

Those five languages provide mates and spouses with a straightforward way to discuss their preferences and create satisfying connections (e.g., “What’s your love language?”). Nevertheless, despite their clinical origin and popularity, the effects of these love languages have not been widely studied academically. More recently, however, research has begun to evaluate their effects in real-world relationships. So, below, we’ll see which languages work, how they impact relationship satisfaction and sex—and why matching really does matter!

Testing Love Languages

Mostova, Stolarski, and Matthews (2022) conducted a study to explore the effects of Chapman’s love languages hypothesis with 100 heterosexual couples. Participants were asked to report the degree to which they expressed each love language to their partner, as well as the level of their own preference to receive each language from their partner. From there, the team calculated the match between each participant’s preferences and the level of their partner’s expression of each love language to them (ranging from 0, a perfect match, to 4, a complete mismatch). Each partner also reported their level of satisfaction with the relationship and their sexual interactions.

Initial results showed that participants considered all love languages important for both expressing and receiving love in their relationship (means from 4.67 to 3.31 on a 1-5 scale). On average, however, some were preferred more than others, with touch as the highest, closely followed by time, then words, service, and gifts. There were also some gender differences, with women wanting to receive more expressions of love in all languages, except acts of service—and being more likely to express their love through quality time.

article continues after advertisement

Despite those few differences, men and women tended to match up well on the language type(s) they wanted to receive and the expressions of love their partner gave to them. When there was a mismatch, however, women tended to want a bit more (especially quality time), whereas men wanted a bit less (except service). Nevertheless, couples shared similar preferences to give and receive acts of service and gifts (indicating assortative mating). When they didn’t share a preference in touch, time, or words, they maintained a satisfying match by giving each other what they wanted anyway.

This desire to give a partner what they wanted was particularly important because Mostova, Stolarski, and Matthews (2022) found that it correlated with both relationship satisfaction and sexual satisfaction. This was especially true for touching, spending time, and words of affirmation. Thus, participants speaking in their partner’s love language (especially when it was important and different from their own) was essential for relationship success—and getting their own needs met in return too. Thus, their experimental results generally supported Chapman’s (1992) initial clinical observations.

Speaking the Same Language

Overall, these results show the importance of mutually satisfying exchange for relationship satisfaction, which I also stress in my book Attraction Psychology (Nicholson, 2022). Put simply, reciprocity and exchange are key. If partners communicate with each other about what they want and meet each other’s needs, then their relationship becomes happier, healthier, and more satisfying. Furthermore, such communication and satisfaction are enhanced by using a partner’s preferred language. So, below, I’ll add a few tips from my book and other articles to help you interact and exchange in their love language better too:

article continues after advertisement

Touch: Research shows that touching your partner routinely has a positive effect on relationship and sexual satisfaction (Clark & Lefkowitz, 2025). More specifically, performing various affectionate behaviors at least once a day (e.g., hugging, kissing, cuddling, holding hands, and caressing) impacts relationship satisfaction, whereas sharing more sensual touching every week or so (e.g., deeply kissing, making out, and erotically caressing) influences sexual satisfaction. So, remember to touch!

Quality Time: Studies also show that sharing exciting activities (e.g., sports, carnival rides, or thrilling movies) sparks attraction and improves satisfaction (Aron, Norman, Aron, McKenna, & Heyman, 2000). Sharing bonding conversations, especially with enthusiastic statements and appreciative responses, increases romance too (McFarland, Jurafsky, & Rawlings, 2013). So, take time to do something exciting together—and then talk about it.

Words of Affirmation: Talking can also be rewarding and reinforcing, especially if it is a compliment. In fact, telling a partner that you notice their contributions to the relationship and appreciate them creates a more rewarding relationship (Dermer, 2006). Supportive comments about specific behaviors also make them more likely to happen again in the future.

Service: Helping a partner in tangible ways increases their satisfaction and often stirs their gratitude (Kubacka, Finkenauer, Rusbult, & Keijsera, 2011). In turn, that gratitude inspires reciprocity, which makes them more likely to meet your needs in return. So, look for ways to be of service—just make sure they appreciate it too!

Gifts: While often practical, gifts send symbolic messages that also stir emotions. So, giving a present is often a great way to mark a special occasion, show affection, indicate appreciation, apologize, or even encourage romance and physical intimacy (Jonason, Tost, & Koenig, 2012). It doesn’t necessarily have to be lavish, but make sure it is thoughtful and considerate of your partner’s interests.

Now go speak their love language—and send your partner a copy of this article, so they know how to speak your love language too!

item.title: Wisdom At Your Core: Discovering the Deepest Ground
item.description:
Spirituality

Wisdom At Your Core: Discovering the Deepest Ground

John Prendergast on his unique approach to "waking down"

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • It's not enough to "wake up" spiritually. To live authentically, we also need to "wake down."
  • As awakening progresses, we naturally experience a process that feels like a descent within to deeper levels.
  • As we process unconscious beliefs and traumatic experiences, we access our true ground, and an abiding trust.
Source: John Prendergast

This is Part One of a two-part series.

John J. Prendergast is a brilliant outlier in the fields of spirituality and mental health. As a teacher, writer, therapist, and retired adjunct professor of psychology, he bridges western psychotherapy with the perennial teachings of nondual philosophy. His unique work focuses on the powerful process of "waking down," which emphasizes embodied insight — the illumination of emotions, relationships, and ordinary life — more than transcendental awareness. The author of several books, including Your Deepest Ground: A Guide to Embodied Spirituality and The Deep Heart: Our Portal to Presence, he offers residential retreats in the U.S. and Europe, as well as online workshops and teaching. In this two-part interview, we talked about the wisdom at our core, and how to tap into our deepest ground.

Mark Matousek: I'd like to begin with your insights into “waking down," a phrase I have never encountered before. What do you mean by waking down?

John Prendergast: I actually borrowed the term “waking down” from Saniel Bonder because it was very resonant for me. We are all familiar with the term waking up, of course. Waking up is actually part of the journey to waking down, which is the realization that you and I are not who we take ourselves to be, (especially not our stories, thoughts, and beliefs). As that realization becomes clear, we often experience a sense of tremendous freedom and space. Frequently, however, the experience tends to localize around and above the head; it has a celestial, sky-like feeling to it. Very often, people believe that's it, but, in fact, this realization is just the beginning. What about everything below the neck? What about the heart? What about the guts? What about the ground? As spiritual realization deepens, there is a descent of awareness. We go from the mind to the heart, then deeper into the unconscious and instinctual dimensions, including archetypal and ancestral material, deep fears of abandonment, engulfment, fragmentation, and then existential dimensions of opening to the vastness of life itself. That's what I mean by waking down.

MM: In your most recent book, you refer to the "ground" as being terra incognita, for the most part. Unexplored territory.

JP: Yes. That is because many spiritual seekers are quite ungrounded. So much of spiritual teaching focuses on transcendence, on aspiring to go "up and out." But the real point of spiritual realization is that it's all here right now, as a human being, in this moment. Waking down is about embodying this understanding; if it's not embodied, it's ungrounded. When this happens, what we tend to see is an acting out of unconscious material. This is all too common among spiritual teachers, students, and communities. For good reason, the psychological community is rather suspicious of the more transcendental spiritual teachings. In those spiritual traditions, we find a dismissal of the value of working closely with one's psychological conditioning. But if we're genuinely interested in human intimacy, and intimacy with our environment, it requires what I call a “descent” of awareness, and an encounter with some of the deepest, darkest, least conscious aspects of who we are — what we often refer to as shadow material — in order to experience ordinary life in a grounded, integrated way.

article continues after advertisement

MM: When did you realize that this terra incognita was going to be so central to your teaching?

JP: It's been a gradual revelation since it was also unknown territory for me. I was following mainstream spiritual disciplines in my twenties, practicing and teaching TM (Transcendental Meditation), going to long meditation courses, doing eight hours of sitting a day, and so on. I could achieve states of quietude and clarity as long as I stayed in my room and wasn't in relationship with anyone. When I was in relationship, I became anxious and realized there was some important need that was not being met. Like a lot of people, I was quite unconscious of what the lower half of my body was doing on a deep and subtle level. I was physically grounded, more or less, but not grounded energetically or emotionally. I saw evidence of this same lack of grounding in other people as well, and also in other spiritual teachings. Eventually, my own love of truth, authenticity, and intimacy simply led me in this direction, as well as to different teachers.

In the early 2000s, after meeting Adyashanti, I really began to understand the importance of waking down. I was on retreat with Adya, who was talking about loosening the existential grip in the gut, when the lights went on and the bells went off. I realized that that was what I needed to be in touch with, the edge I needed to explore, and practicing as a depth psychotherapist for 35 years, I saw the same phenomenon in the people I worked with. The locus of the problem is in the gut — the solar plexus — as well as at the base of the spine, where there is often a strong lock around safety, security, and survival. As my own system opened, I was able to sense the closedness or openness in others pretty accurately. I've found that when people recognize this in themselves and don't dismiss it, the system begins to open, and the ground begins to flower. It’s a gradual process.

MM: Can you say more about the "lock" around safety and survival that localizes at the base of the spine?

JP: Absolutely. The work I do includes the recognition of what's sometimes called the "energy body." In other words, the subtle somatic sensations that we experience. There's the gross physical body we all know about, as well as the energetic (or subtle) level of sensitivity that is well known in Eastern contemplative traditions. As our sense of the physical body opens, we realize that it's not just this dense object, and begin to feel energy centers in our body. At the base of the spine is the root chakra — root meaning "at the base." The primary function of the root chakra concerns security; when we feel unsafe, that energy center tends to lock and shut down. There's a pulling in, a pulling up, a tendency to be vigilant and to look out for danger. This is often the experience of people who've been traumatized, for instance. They live in their heads or out of their body, constantly scanning their surroundings in search of danger.

article continues after advertisement

As we begin to feel safer, we're able to drop further down and a different kind of opening emerges. As issues that have triggered our sense of danger are seen through, felt through, sensed through, the system naturally begins to relax. We discover that what we had taken to be the ground is not the ground. In other words, we took this contraction to be our ground. "This is who I am, this is what I stand on." Then, as we begin to open, we realize that it was false ground, provisional ground. It's not our deepest ground. We discover that there is, in fact, a huge, spacious dimension beneath it. When you open to this foundational space, ground becomes available for the full flowering of our humanity. This is why waking down is so important and interesting! Because it's so buried and unconscious, and not adequately recognized in the spiritual traditions. That’s why I wrote the book.

Stay tuned for Part Two of this interview.

item.title: Fraternities, Masculinity, and the Bystander Problem
item.description:
Sex

Fraternities, Masculinity, and the Bystander Problem

How group norms within the Greek system can shape masculinity and women's safety.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • The desire to be part of group can stop fraternity members from calling out unacceptable behaviour.
  • Men should take responsibility for their own behaviour, particularly if that behaviour is harmful.
  • Those with higher status in a fraternity should act as a positive role model for those below them.

Recent headlines about behaviour within college fraternities have reignited a familiar debate about frat culture. Repeated incidents of misogyny, harassment, and sexual misconduct suggest that fraternities can foster unhealthy and, at times, deeply harmful group norms.

At their best, fraternities have the potential to model positive masculinity by creating communities where young men support, encourage, and challenge one another to be their best selves (Matthews, 2022). However, at their worst, loyalty to the group can be seen as more important than responsibility to others, particularly women. This creates a culture where problematic behaviour, including sexual misconduct, is too often excused, minimised, or even encouraged (McCready, Schutts & McCreary, 2022).

Change requires action at every level, from how men reflect on their own behaviour to how friends, fraternities, colleges, and wider communities respond when boundaries are crossed. Here are 5 places to start:

1. Men Must Take Responsibility for Their Own Behaviour

Those who engage in sexual misconduct are responsible for their actions and should be held accountable for the choices they make. However, this alone is not enough. We must also examine the attitudes, behaviours, and social norms that make such misconduct possible, by creating a culture where such behaviour is deemed to be acceptable.

This requires men to honestly reflect on their own beliefs and behaviour. Do they view women as equal human beings with their own wants, boundaries, and autonomy or do they see them primarily as potential sexual partners, conquests, or sources of status among their peers?

The objectification of women often starts with everyday attitudes that reduce them to bodies rather than people, and as something to pursue, obtain, rank, or discuss, rather than individuals deserving of dignity and respect. Positive masculinity requires men to reject these attitudes and recognise that consent, respect, and empathy are not obstacles to relationships.

2. Men Need to Challenge Their Friends

Most men have the capacity to recognise sexist language, degrading humour, and boundary violations, including instances of sexual misconduct. However, all too often these behaviours are normalised, excused, or ignored, as the desire to be part of the group outweighs the willingness to intervene.

De Fazio et all (2024) highlighted the specific need for tailored bystander intervention programmes within the college Greek system, due to their increased risk of sexual misconduct. The strong social bonds with a fraternity can present a challenge for active bystandership in fraternities, particularly for those who are lower in the hierarchy.

article continues after advertisement

Bystander programmes tailored to fraternities should therefore include a range of direct and indirect interventions, including disclosing concerns confidentially to trusted staff, bringing in allies and the use of distraction or interruption to stop a situation progressing. This way bystanders can still act, while avoiding directly challenging their peers.

3. Fraternities Must Redefine What Brotherhood Means

Brotherhood should mean helping one another become better men, not providing cover when someone behaves badly. A healthy fraternity should never reward misogyny, sexual bravado, or disrespect toward women.

If the current situation is to improve, the definition of brotherhood must expand beyond blindly agreeing with friends or standing by when they do something wrong. It means caring enough to call a friend out, holding them accountable for their actions, and becoming an active bystander when someone's safety or well-being is at risk.

Baggetta et al (2024) noted the potential for fraternities to develop civil society in their members and encourage them to be positive, supportive members of society, but only if members were actively seeking to achieve this. As in most groups, the members with the greatest status set the tone. This offers the opportunity for those at the top of the hierarchy to model positive masculinity and respectful behaviour for those below them. This then sets the standard for how others should behave. Unfortunately, the challenge is often convincing those at the top to voluntarily give up the perceived "perks" of their status, even when those perks involve misogyny, abuse, or sexual misconduct.

article continues after advertisement

4. Colleges Must Be Prepared to Act

Colleges and universities have a responsibility to act. Where evidence of misconduct exists, there must be meaningful consequences that reflect the seriousness of the behaviour.

Having perpetrators write essays or undertake brief suspensions can make the problem worse, if they’re perceived as overly lenient or designed simply to educate offenders rather than punish their behaviour. This can then undermine confidence in the reporting process and send the message that the harm caused is not being taken seriously.

When harmful behaviour occurs, the priority should not be protecting reputations, organisations, traditions, or influential groups. It should be establishing the facts, prioritising student safety, holding individuals accountable where appropriate, and ensuring that those affected receive justice and support. Clear policies, consistent enforcement, meaningful sanctions, and measures that prioritise the safety and well-being of those affected are essential if institutions are to build trust and create genuinely safe campus environments.

5. Recognise That Women's Safety Is Not Just a Women's Issue

Discussions about sexual misconduct often treats it as just a women's issue, because in most cases (though not all) it’s women who are affected by it. The reality is that the epidemic of sexual violence within university campuses is everybody’s responsibility to address.

Campuses should be a safe, supportive environment for all students to learn, yet all too often, particular groups of students, most notably women, are forced to adapt their behaviour to avoid risk. Men have a critical role to play in challenging harmful attitudes, reshaping group norms, and setting expectations for how others should be treated. In other words, as well as being a decent person yourself, positive masculinity is about helping to create a culture where other men are expected to be better too.

The bottom line is that many parts of the fraternity experience are profoundly positive and play an important role in positive masculinity. This includes including male bonding, friendship, identity, and belonging. Problems emerge however, when loyalty to the group becomes more important than individual accountability. In such an environment, men can encourage one another's worst behaviour rather than challenge it. So going forward, the challenge for fraternities is simple: Stop protecting the men who cross the line and start protecting the people they harm.

item.title: 12 Vital Things to Do to Assert Your Self-Respect
item.description:
Assertiveness

12 Vital Things to Do to Assert Your Self-Respect

Self-respect isn't just something you feel; it's something you practice.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • Self-respect is exemplified through behavior: how you set boundaries, communicate, and the choices you make.
  • Assertiveness means honoring your own needs and rights while respecting those of others.
  • Every time you act in alignment with your values, you reinforce the message that you have worth and matter.
Source: Edward Howell / Unsplash

Self-respect is exemplified through your behavior toward yourself and others. Psychological definitions of self-respect emphasize regard and proactive action toward fortifying one's values, dignity, and worth.

You can believe you deserve respect while repeatedly chasing validation, avoiding confronting issues directly, saying yes when you feel otherwise, tolerating mistreatment, abandoning your values, or silencing your needs.

The question becomes: Do your actions demonstrate to you that you have intrinsic worth and innately matter?

Here are 12 ways to practice self-respect:

1. Stop Chasing Validation Externally

Look for validation within. Your opinion of yourself matters most. You are only in competition with yourself. Use yourself as a barometer to formulate goals, assess progress, and to evaluate your needs.

2. Say No When You Feel Otherwise

Every reluctant and forced yes can become an act of self-abandonment. You don't need to justify declining something. Try: "I can't commit to that" or "I'm not able to do that at this time."

Assertiveness is different than aggressiveness. It means expressing your needs directly while also maintaining kindness, thoughtfulness, and respect for others. Recent research examining assertiveness conceptualizes assertiveness as involving cognitive, emotional, and behavioral skills that can be practiced and strengthened (Watanabe, 2025).

3. Avoid Overexplaining Your Decisions

Notice when you're explaining yourself to obtain permission. This usually comes with discomfort when you think or perceive that someone is uncomfortable with your decision or isn't understanding or agreeing with you. You can make a thoughtful decision that isn't approved of. Others’ disappointment doesn't automatically mean your decision isn't thoughtful or is wrong.

Self-respect can sometimes mean tolerating being misunderstood, disagreed with, or met with discomfort.

4. Setting and Sticking to Your Boundaries

Setting a boundary is about determining your parameters and expectations, and how a violation of them will be handled. Try: "This is making me uncomfortable. If you continue yelling at me, I'm going to make the choice to end the conversation."

Ensure that you maintain and reinforce your boundaries. If you continually abandon your boundaries, you communicate that your boundaries are loose and negotiable.

5. Take Promises You Make to Yourself Seriously

Self-trust matters significantly. If you don’t make enough of an effort to follow through with yourself, you may need to ask yourself why others are more important to you than yourself.

If you repeatedly promise yourself that you'll finish a task, exercise, opt out of an unhealthy situation, or stop engaging in a destructive pattern, and continually don't follow through, you weaken confidence and legitimacy in your own word.

6. Express Yourself When Something Matters to You

Self-respect says, "You deserve to be heard and understood, unequivocally." Research across seven countries found that greater self-respect was associated with greater assertiveness and fewer depressive symptoms (Renger et al., 2023).

Try: "That hurt me, "We have a difference of opinion," or "I need something different." Speaking up doesn't guarantee you'll get the response you want or need. It means you're committing to no longer disappearing, avoiding, or distracting yourself because of your fear that you won't be attended to or to preserve harmony.

7. Stop Chasing People

Self-respect asks: Am I investing disproportionately in someone who repeatedly isn’t showing up for me? Respecting yourself means directing your energy toward healthy, secure, and nurturing relationships that positively impact your nervous system.

Emerging research suggests that self-respect is shaped through our experiences of being treated with respect (Renger et al., 2026). Intentionally surround yourself with people who treat you with worthiness, kindness, and care.

8. Speak to Yourself Respectfully

You can't expect to assert self-respecting behavior if you continually demean and criticize yourself. Research on self-compassion defines it as responding supportively to ourselves during inadequacy, failure, and suffering. Evidence also challenges the misconception that self-compassion undermines motivation. It's quite the opposite, it compels it (Neff, 2023).

Self-compassion, accountability, and self-respect can coexist. Instead of: "I'm such an idiot," replace it with: "I made a mistake. What lesson can I learn from it?"

9. Don't Betray Your Values

Don’t abandon who you are and what’s important to you. This can come at a steep psychological cost.

Self-respect asks: Am I making this choice because it reflects who and how I want to be, or because I'm afraid of someone's reaction or to avoid an uncomfortable emotion?

10. Stop Accepting Repeated Disrespect, Even from Someone You Love

You can care deeply about someone and still decide that certain behaviors aren't acceptable. You don't need to prove your compassion and worth by endlessly tolerating disregard, manipulation, criticism, or dishonesty.

Self-respect asks: "What happens to me in this relationship?" Consider whether you’re aligned with your values and whether you’re showing up as your best self.

11. Be Willing to Disappoint Others

This may be one of the hardest practices of all. Sometimes asserting self-respect means someone won't appreciate your boundary or disagree with your decision.

If you've spent years organizing your behavior around others' comfort, choosing yourself may initially “feel” selfish. It isn’t selfish if you’re consciously considering the needs and desires of others but mindfully choosing to be self-honoring.

Self-respect doesn't mean believing you're more important than everyone else. It means finally recognizing that you're not less important either. At times, you recognize that your needs appropriately take precedence.

12. Communicate Issues Directly

Communicate directly and effectively. Be cautious about acting out your subconscious or unconscious perceptions, attitudes, or judgments.

Your self-respect dictates that you avoid communicating indirectly, passive-aggressively, or expecting someone to read your mind. Cultivating self-respect includes enhancing how you approach yourself and others in regard to behavior and communication.

Building Self-Respect Is Cumulative

Self-respect is strengthened through a plethora of small decisions. It’s based on the no you finally say, the conversation you stop avoiding, the promises you keep to yourself, and the values you refuse to compromise.

Take the time to continually contemplate what you would do differently today if you acted like your self-respect truly mattered and was consistently honored.

item.title: Additional Capabilities of a Comprehensive Laughter Theory
item.description:
Laughter

Additional Capabilities of a Comprehensive Laughter Theory

The difficulties of constructing a meaningful, all-inclusive theory of laughter.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • Laughter appears a rather simple, almost automatic behavior, but scholars have struggled to explain it.
  • Most theoretical approaches answer some of the questions raised but fall short of being comprehensive.
  • There are several topics related to laughter and humor that an exhaustive theory must tackle.

In two prior posts, here and here, I reported on some of the results from an article I wrote for the European Journal of Humour Research titled “Essential Attributes of a Comprehensive Theory of Laughter” (Simon, 2020). That paper cataloged a range of topics scholars have investigated about laughter over the past four decades and revealed why a single, “unified” theory of laughter and humor has remained so elusive.

Previously reported themes

Source: Juliane Monari Fotografia / Pexels

Part One of this series reported about a dozen themes into which the various topics could be categorized. Last month, in Part Two, I described a dozen more questions, including those relating to laughter’s acoustic structure; the message it conveys, if any; how it serves as an indicator of personality, health, and status; laughter’s relationship with smiling; why it has a dual nature, sometimes friendly, other times mean spirited; laughter’s evolutionary origins; why we express volitional (feigned) laughter; why laughter is sometime contagious; and whether there are different varieties, embarrassed, nervous, excited, etc.; why it varies in intensity and duration; why laughter and humor is used by bullies; and laughter’s close association with tickling. Below are the remaining themes encountered during my original search.

More themes various experts have addressed

Sense of Humor. What do we mean by the term “sense of humor”? What distinguishes a “good” one from a “poor” one? Are there objective criteria?

Instinctive vs. Learned. To what extent is laughter an instinctive behavior, a culturally determined behavior, or some combination of both? What factors influence what we find amusing?

Computational Laughter and Humor. Are laughter and humor traits that can be accurately simulated through the use of artificial intelligence? Is this achievable in the absence of a comprehensive understanding of both? What are the downsides posed by such a capability, if any?

Source: Ruslan Sikunov / Pexels

Relationship to Crying (Sobbing). There are instances in which individuals can laugh and cry simultaneously, or transition almost seamlessly from one to the other. What is the relationship, if any, between these two behaviors? Why are their outward expressions so similar?

Laughing at Ourselves. We seem to laugh “with” and “at” others quite naturally, but there are those instances in which we also laugh while focused on our own behavior. It can be the result of our failures as well as our triumphs. What accounts for this self-reflective laughter? Why do we sometimes make ourselves the butt of our own humor?

In Response to Positive Realizations. We laugh at our and others’ foibles, but there are also moments in which we respond to displays of exceptional skill and good fortune as well. What is amusing about great performances and lucky breaks?

The Evolution of Laughter. With respect to our great ape ancestors having a similar expression, for those theories that maintain laughter originated millions of years prior to the advent of our species, what accounts for the differences we observe between our laugh response and that of other species? We laugh at many things great apes simply do not. Why would this be the case?

Laughter's Relationship to Play. Laughter and play often go hand-in-hand, not just for children, but adults as well. What is it about play behavior that triggers participants, and even observers, to engage in laughter? What factors tend to inhibit laughter when it is not present?

Influence of Drugs. Some drugs, most famously nitrous oxide (“laughing gas”), promote laughter. What effects do such chemicals have on the brain and body that might, in turn, initiate this reaction?

Animals/Inanimate Objects. We do not only laugh with and at other people, but also other species. Pets, especially, foster laughter almost as readily as children. Why would this be so, especially if one’s theory assumes laughter is a signal? Presumably, other than perhaps the great apes, they would not understand whatever message we might be sending.

Source: Nicolas Villalobos / Pexels

Other objectives of a comprehensive theory

If answering all these questions weren’t challenging enough, there are several other qualities scholars look for in a truly robust theory of laughter. First among these, a theory must be logically consistent. This means the answer given to one question can’t conflict with that given for another question. If you maintain laughter is a species-wide, purely reflexive physical response to certain stimuli, you can’t also conclude variations in our laugh response will be substantially influenced by, for example, one’s personal history or current emotional disposition.

Another highly prized quality of any newcomer to the scene would be an ability to explain why its competitors seem correct but are not, or are at least not complete. Precisely why do superiority theory, incongruity theory, tension relief theory, play theory, etc. appear viable accounts for laughter, but ultimately fall short?

Finally, as with any scientific theory, a comprehensive account needs to be falsifiable—the ability to test any hypotheses which logically follow from the theory’s fundamental assertions. If you claim laughter’s main function is to communicate “superiority” or reduce “tension,” but have no means of objectively defining and measuring such parameters, there is no hope of being proven wrong, thus no way of establishing one explanation as being better than another. This is, ultimately, the driving force that makes the scientific method so powerful.

item.title: What Family Cutoffs Say About Our Society
item.description:
Family Dynamics

What Family Cutoffs Say About Our Society

Are families really falling apart or does estrangement indicate something else?

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • There is little evidence to suggest that family estrangement is an out of control "epidemic" or catastrophe.
  • Researchers have found that while estrangement does affect many people, it is often temporary.
  • Redefining what family means and who constitutes family can be an empowering and healthy process.
Source: Marek Studzinski/Unsplash

What is family estrangement? Gaining a lot of attention lately, family estrangement is the creation of distance from one or more family members. What causes estrangement? Studies point to individual- and family-level variables such as substance use, excessive drinking, mental health issues, various forms of abuse and trauma, boundary violations, and separation and divorce. These are common and legitimate reasons for family members to pause and reconsider if and how they wish to remain connected. Further, family estrangement and post-traumatic stress—particularly complex PTSD (CPTSD)—often intersect, acting as both a cause and a protective response to prolonged trauma in the home. These and other reasons are certainly valid grounds to initiate estrangement.

Is estrangement an out-of-control epidemic? In his new book, Families We Lose, sociologist Rin Reczek (2026) thoroughly rejects the hyperbole of an estrangement “epidemic” or the moral panic that has taken center stage in the cultural zeitgeist. Popular newspapers, magazines, and social influencers frame a decision of “no contact” as representing total disrespect for the value of the traditional family and a refusal to defer to our elders. But is estrangement really just adults choosing willy-nilly not to honor their mother and father and abandon their families?

Reczek says no and reports there’s no evidence that we are anywhere near becoming a society without families. He conducted a longitudinal study that found that of those who reported estrangement in one of a series of survey waves, 81 percent of mothers and 69 percent of fathers were back in contact with their child in subsequent waves, most often within two years (Reczek and colleagues, 2023). Corroborating this finding, Becker and Hank (2022) concluded that most people who had experienced estrangement had only one acute period of it over 10 years, suggesting that estrangement is often temporary. Therefore, pearl-clutching around an “imminent catastrophe” may be over the top. Reczek (2026) adds that estrangement rates don’t even come close to divorce rates or dissolution of romantic relationships, and thus do not qualify as an all-out disaster.

Estrangement is not destroying families. “Family estrangement is not the cause of family breakdown; it is the consequence” or “outcome of family members being on fundamentally different pages—no, books—on what it means to live every day as a family” (Reczek, 2026, p. 5). What’s he getting at? Reczek (2026) invites us to look beyond specific personal circumstances as the root cause of estrangement and to consider a broader theme: Differing notions of “the cultural meaning of family life” (p. 16), and who constitutes “family.”

article continues after advertisement

There is an ongoing clash in American society between compulsory kinship, where the family of origin must be forever sustained as the center of everyone’s life, and democratized kinship, wherein chosen intimacy features “equity, autonomy, and self-development.” Reczek (2026) notes that over the past century or so, intimacy culture has moved from the organizing principle of legal and economic compulsory ties through the patriarchal institution of close marriage based on personal growth, satisfaction, relational equity, and the available options of dissolution and divorce. Contemporary relationships involve self-reflective and self-determining processes and the possibility of making decisions and taking actions in one’s life without a threat of coercion, manipulation, and abuse (Reczek, 2026, p. 18).

Instead of a “family killer,” estrangement can be thought of as affording one a moratorium, a period of reflection, permitting a transition to a more democratized form of kinship. Redoing or reworking what family means can allow an escape from oppressive relations and from having to bear the brunt of coercive power in a family of origin where the ties that bind do so in disempowering ways. Thus, estrangement may be a step toward reconceptualizing family by negotiating relationships—demonstrating equality, choice, and expression of mutual respect. You decide what family means to you, and who is family. That doesn’t sound like a disaster at all.

item.title: Beyond the Break Room: When Work Friends Become Real Friends
item.description:
Friends

Beyond the Break Room: When Work Friends Become Real Friends

Here's why your next close friend may already be sitting right down the hall.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • We spend so much time at work that it's well worth befriending the people we like working with.
  • The people we see everyday often become the people we value most, especially when we depend on them at work.
  • Strong workplace friendships grow from small, low-risk steps, not through sudden intimacy or TMI dumping.
  • Clear boundaries allow work friendships to flourish both personally and professionally.

Most of us spend more waking hours with coworkers than with neighbors, friends, and sometimes even family members. Given that reality, it's not surprising that workplace relationships can become some of the most meaningful connections we create. Yet many people hesitate to move a work friendship beyond office walls because they feel uncertain about where the line between colleague and friend should be drawn.

The truth is that work friendships occupy a unique space in our social lives. They're formed around shared tasks, common goals, and mutual experiences rather than shared histories or lifestyles. Unlike personal friendships, which often grow from common interests, values, or life circumstances, work friendships begin because two people happen to share the same professional environment.

But sometimes those workplace connections evolve into something deeper.

Why Work Friends Matter

Research consistently suggests that having positive social connections at work contributes to greater job satisfaction, lower stress, and a stronger sense of belonging (Birmingham et al., 2024; Weir, 2024). A trusted coworker can provide emotional support during difficult projects, be a sounding board for challenging decisions, and help us navigate workplace dynamics. They can also offer insights we might miss because they see the organization from a different perspective.

Work friends also understand aspects of our lives that others don't. They witness the daily pressures we face, understand organizational challenges, and appreciate the victories and frustrations that come with our jobs. When something goes wrong at work, a supportive colleague often needs very little explanation to understand why we're struggling.

And because familiarity plays such a powerful role in relationship formation, friendships frequently develop among the people we see most often. Psychologists have long recognized that repeated exposure tends to increase liking. Simply put, spending time together creates opportunities for connection. We tend to like the people we see most often anyway, so we might as well befriend them. Many of our colleagues already occupy a significant portion of our daily lives.

Why Some Work Friendships Grow and Others Don't

Not every enjoyable workplace relationship develops into a genuine friendship. Some remain congenial but professional, while others gradually expand into connections that extend beyond “office hours.”

Difficult situations and workplace crises can bring coworkers closer together, and when we feel we “click” with someone, that may be a sign that a genuine friendship is waiting to happen. Shared challenges can bring out coworkers’ most appealing traits, such as reliability, empathy, humor, and resilience. This can help us see one another in a different light and open the door for deeper connections.

Several factors that encourage work friendships to deepen include:

  • Gradual self-disclosure
  • Shared experiences, especially during stressful periods
  • Discovering common interests outside work
  • Spending time together in non-work settings
  • A natural sense of that interpersonal "click"

How to Test the Waters

For many adults, making a friend feels surprisingly vulnerable. When a potential friend is also a coworker, the risk can feel even greater.

Rather than making a dramatic leap from colleague to close friend, consider taking small, low-pressure steps.

  • Invite them to grab coffee or lunch one-on-one. Suggest a brief walk after work. Mention a shared interest and see whether they'd like to attend an event related to it.
  • Another useful approach is sharing a small personal story and observing whether the other person reciprocates. Friendships typically develop through a gradual exchange of personal information, with both people slowly revealing more about themselves over time.

Think of friendship development as opening a series of doors, rather than throwing open the entire house. Allow someone into your story a little at a time and let the relationship unfold naturally.

What Gets in the Way?

Despite the potential benefits, workplace friendships come with unique challenges. People may worry about oversharing, becoming the subject of office gossip, or creating awkwardness if the friendship changes. Power differences between supervisors and employees can introduce additional complications. Even among peers, concerns about professionalism may make some people hesitant to get too close.

These are legitimate concerns.

In healthy work friendships, both friendship and professionalism can coexist. Being friends doesn't eliminate workplace expectations, accountability, or boundaries. In fact, clear boundaries often strengthen workplace friendships rather than weaken them.

The Importance of Boundaries

As work friendships deepen, some conversations are best kept outside the office. Highly personal discussions about relationships, family conflicts, health concerns, finances, or deeply held political or religious beliefs are better shared over coffee than in the office. The goal isn't secrecy but discretion.

A useful rule of thumb is this: If you’d be comfortable with other colleagues overhearing the conversation, continue the discussion. If not, save it for coffee after work.

Similarly, work-related disagreements should still be handled professionally, even when they involve a friend. Healthy work friendships can survive differences of opinion precisely because both people understand that professionalism still comes first on the job.

For Those Who Prefer to Keep Work and Personal Lives Separate

Not everyone wants coworkers to become close friends, and that's okay. Meaningful workplace relationships don't require blurred boundaries. You can enjoy supportive, rewarding connections with colleagues while maintaining clear distinctions between your professional and personal life.

At the same time, it's worth recognizing that the people we spend the most time with can become important sources of companionship, support, and belonging. In a world where many adults report feeling lonely and disconnected (APA, 2025), workplace friendships offer a valuable opportunity to build meaningful connections. Work is work, and when stress builds, having a trusted work friend to talk things through is a gift. Whether the friendship stays on-site or grows beyond it, those connections can make our professional and personal lives richer.

You don't have to invite every coworker into your personal life. But if a trusted colleague seems like someone you'd enjoy knowing beyond the office, it may be worth taking a small step outside the break room.

Sometimes the best friendships begin in places we’d least expect to find them, and your next great friendship may be sitting right down the hall.

item.title: The Invisible Weight of Leadership
item.description:
Leadership

The Invisible Weight of Leadership

Leadership is sustainable when we care for the person behind the position.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • Leadership can feel lonely as more people depend on you for answers and stability.
  • Self-care must be part of how leaders live and lead, not something saved for vacations.
  • Leaders need people who know them beyond their titles, accomplishments, and responsibilities.

Last week I was in California sitting in a room full of Chief Probation Officers. I had gone there to talk about grief, leadership, and self-care following the sudden death of one of their colleagues. But I didn't start by talking about grief. I asked them to finish one sentence: “You know you're a Chief when…” This allowed them to speak freely, laugh, and share common experiences only they understand. A common theme arose that is worth sharing, which is the higher you move up in leadership, the fewer people you can call on when you are the one who needs help.

I’m currently the first Black Director of Rutgers University Counseling, Alcohol and Other Drug Assistance Program & Psychiatric Services (CAPS). I have a team of almost 60 individuals. Although I try my best to flatten the hierarchy and share leadership, the honest truth is that when things go down, budgets get cut, and tough decisions are made, I need to be the steady force in the organization. As a leader, people become so accustomed to our strength that they forget the strength we display costs us something. Sometimes, we forget too.

The Invisible Weight of Leadership

I told the Chiefs that we spend so much time investing in others that it is time we held up a mirror to ourselves and invested in our own well-being. I was intentional about talking about the invisible weight that comes with being people like us: responsibility, emotional labor, visibility, and isolation.

Responsibility is probably the most obvious. Every day, we are responsible for other people, the functioning of a department or system, budgets, others’ safety and well-being. Even when I delegate a task, I still feel responsible for the outcome. We know that when things hit the fan, the buck stops with us. That’s a lot of pressure.

The Invisible Weight of Leadership
Source: AI generated

Then there is emotional labor. Being in a leadership role often requires us to manage our emotions while helping everyone else manage theirs. You can “not be ok” and still have to lead a meeting. You can be grieving and still have people waiting outside your office who need something from you.

The higher we rise in leadership, the more people watch us. Our words, our decisions, sometimes even our facial expressions matter! I have a trusted colleague friend who often reminds me of my “face” when I am in meetings. People interpret our silence, our tone, and what we did or did not say. We do not give ourselves grace, because others rarely do.

Last but not least, there is isolation, which is the part few people truly understand. There are things we as leaders simply cannot discuss with everyone around us, from confidential personnel issues to organizational uncertainty and difficult decisions. This creates what I think of as the leadership paradox: The higher we rise, the more people depend on us and the fewer people we can depend on.

Who can support me, the person everyone else depends on?

Unpacking the Invisible Leadership Backpack

While with the Chiefs last week, I had us examine this question: What is in my leadership backpack? I explained that we all carry this invisible backpack everywhere we go. In it can be many things: every difficult decision, every crisis, every loss, every responsibility. Over the years, things begin to accumulate, which makes the weight we carry even heavier.

Now I pose this question to you, my reader… what have you added to your backpack over the years? What have you never taken out? What belongs to me and what belongs to someone else?

The Leadership Backpack
Source: AI Image

I find that many of my trainings with leaders and organizations are trainings I wish I had myself. I took the time in this training right along with the Chiefs to truly answer these questions for myself. We have Plans A, B, and C for our departments, our budgets, and our employees, but do we have a plan for ourselves?

Self-care for leaders often gets put on the back burner. We carry the false idea that self-care is vacations, massages, spa days, or taking time off. And listen, I am not against any of these things! But if our entire self-care plan depends on getting away from our lives, we need to talk about that. Because eventually, we have to come back.

In my book, Healer, Heal Thyself, I discuss psychological wellness as more than simply avoiding stress. Self-care is not a reward for surviving your job. It is part of how you sustainably do your job. And it has to work on an ordinary Tuesday, not only during the seven days a year when your out-of-office message is on.

4 Questions for Sustainable Leadership

  1. Recover: What genuinely restores me? This isn't about what should restore you, but what actually helps you feel like yourself again. Be honest about what works for you rather than what you think wellness is supposed to look like.
  2. Protect: What do I need to take back? Maybe it's your sleep or your exercise routine. If you’re like me, maybe it’s your weekend or simply an hour when nobody can reach you. I learned to be intentional by taking back what is mine and what my job was not paying me for.
  3. Notice: How do I know when I'm not okay? We need to know our early warning signs. Maybe you become more impatient, withdraw from other people, or start working even longer hours. Knowing your early warning signs allows you to intervene before you get to your breaking point.
  4. Connect: Who really knows me? Not your title. Not your accomplishments. You. The best thing I could have done for myself was actively engage with my fellow Big Ten Counseling Center Directors who also carry the weight of leading large counseling centers. Additionally, I have my besties who have known me since elementary school, before the degrees, the titles, and the accolades. Do you have someone who asks how you are doing without immediately following the question with something they need from you? I truly hope this for you.

Final Takeaway

Leaders are extraordinarily good at making plans. We make operational plans, succession plans, emergency plans, budget plans, and five-year strategic plans. But when was the last time you made one for you?

Trust me, it doesn't have to be elaborate. You can start by identifying your early warning signs, what helps you recover, the people you can genuinely lean on, one boundary you need to protect, and one thing you are willing to do differently in the next 30 days.

Leadership will always carry weight. The goal isn't to become better at carrying the weight, nor is it to pretend the weight isn't there. The goal is to recognize what you're carrying, understand what it is doing to you, and make sure there are places where you can put some of it down. Because behind the position, the accomplishments, the decisions, and the person everyone else depends on, there is still a person, YOU. And YOU deserve care, too.

item.title: The Melodious Love That Keeps Us Well
item.description:
Relationships

The Melodious Love That Keeps Us Well

Just as we sing a melody to life, we breathe daily intentions to sustain health.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • Health improves with emotional resilience.
  • When we consciously capture joy as a daily practice, we cultivate healthier internal systems.
  • Love is being willing to lose part of ourselves to be part of the collective.

An older family member rants to me that her life has never been busier—because she is drowning in too many remedies and healthy habits!

Wellness can seem like an all-consuming challenge. The more options we are given in the profitable market of endless youth and vitality, the less bandwidth we feel we have to process, and the more tools we need to plan the long journey ahead.

We need to find motivation and purpose for doing the sustained work that is required for staying healthy. Part 2 of this 3-part series on Musical Health ended with the idea that learning how to ease up on effort is crucial for that sustainability. This article continues with recognizing the love for life, others, and ourselves that motivates and multiplies our resolve.

Working backwards then, we need to pursue the environment and community that will give us motivation and resources to find sustainability.

Before that, the prerequisite is to be able to capture joy and link a sense of purpose to the effort.

And that would be preceded by having the emotional resilience to be aware of how we relate to our health from moment to moment and what we need to recalibrate as we navigate life’s uncertainties.

Music offers us a pleasurable way to work on that emotional resilience, without which our efforts in healthcare and caregiving would be futile.

Health Improves with Emotional Resilience

Health is a holistic state of physical, mental, emotional, spiritual, and social well-being that happens when we function optimally and sustainably. Biomarkers like cortisol, oxytocin, and DHEA, improve with musical engagement, which helps us find spiritual motivation. The Health and Retirement Study, following nearly 7,000 adults over 50 for eight years, found that a higher sense of purpose in life predicted a lower likelihood of a inflammation marker over time. Meditation, prayer, stillness, and awareness of our mood - all of which are enhanced through music - are the mediums through which we pursue a more harmonious homeostasis - the body's internal stability.

Musical engagement and music-based interventions (MBIs) sustain wellness efforts by promoting the emotional resilience that leads to positive age beliefs. Making music with our bodies and voices physiologically exercise more diverse parts of the brain than any other activity.

When we can integrate life’s challenges into a fully processed personal story, we become more resilient.

The Practice of Capturing Joy

To be sure, we cannot save a loved one from terminal illness just by thinking it. But until I faced death alongside loved ones, I never realized how much social determinants and emotional determinants directly factor into physical health, creating a ripple effect on all the accompanying variables.

article continues after advertisement

Yale Prof. Becca Levy set out to show the impact of mindset in aging in her recent study of geriatric health. 45.15% of persons over the retirement age of 65 improved in cognitive and/or physical function over the period of the study, and it was “positive age beliefs” that predicted these two types of improvement for up to 12 years later.

In my piano studio, I have taught seniors who present as 10, 20 years younger than their physical age. They all shared the ability to capture joy in learning new things, in trying out physical challenges on the piano, and in connecting with the emotions of the music.

Coming together in collective learning environments creates a space for us to care for each other, which in turn creates purpose and energy. Theodosius Dobzhansky, a Russian population geneticist, found that instead of genetic mutation and natural selection being at odds, they join in a synthesis: “The fittest may also be the gentlest, because survival often requires mutual help and cooperation.”(Dobzhansky, 1962)

This quote is not just about escaping physical danger to stay alive, but also to create favorable systems that help us to thrive as conscious beings. It has been referenced by many thought leaders including Stephen W. Porges regarding the experience of safety (mentioned in Part 2). Stephen Nachmanovitch in his book Free Play: Improvisation in Life and Art” links musical improvisation to the practice of choosing to look for abundance. In faith practice, this would be called discipleship.

Connecting with Others

How well we find that abundance and joy impact our physical bodies. Holt-Lunstad's landmark 2010 analysis covering over 300,000 participants found that people with strong social bonds were about 50 percent less likely to die over a given follow-up period. Our actual and perceived reality can spiritually change with music as a portal to greater truths.

Conversely, former U.S. Surgeon General Dr. Vivek Murthy reports that people who feel loneliness face “the mortality impact of social disconnection is on par with smoking or obesity.”

In my recent Musical Health Benefit Concert, I paired a Chopin Nocturne for solo piano with a love sonnet by the Italian poet Petrarca. The speaker of the poem, paired simultaneously with the emotions of Frédéric Chopin the musical poet, moves through different emotional revelations. In the poem, his strong desires for a woman who rejects him transform him into restlessness and outburst, acceptance, and finally, peace. Although the poem is a monologue, its power lies in being shared with a reader, just as music comes to live when it is heard, and we experience health when we we connect with someone.

article continues after advertisement

Love is Being Willing to Lose Part of Ourselves to Something Bigger

While American popular culture loves to present winners who dominate, through Chopin’s piece and this poem, we experience that when we truly love, we become willing to lose for the sake of our love or our cause. This is why caring for each other is so powerful; we strengthen each other’s ability to accept reality so that we can live at our fullest internal capacity, whatever the reality is.

While terminal disease is not going to vanish if we feel enough joy, we can still be truly healthy even when dying. Take Senator Ben Sasse, for example—he expresses an ease, despite chronic pain and imminent death, that is rare even in people with physically perfect health. He is so connected with the flow of love around him, both human and divine, that he can choose to yield life without giving up joy.

Radical acceptance of all possible outcomes—including loss—is the beginning of fully living. It frees us from the fear-driven instinct to hedge our bets. Paradoxically it also improves our best chances of achieving our aspirations.

Mini Musical Meditation

Allow your mind to bring up a worst-case scenario. Can you hold that emotion through a few slow breaths? Is there a musical sound, chord, song, that can serve as a vessel to hold it for you? Can you listen as that sound eventually fades away? Can you wait for the stillness that follows, the space that allows regeneration?

The love and mutual care in our lives, not grit alone, motivate and sustain our efforts to stay healthy.

item.title: What Schools Can Do to Prevent Suicides
item.description:
Suicide

What Schools Can Do to Prevent Suicides

The solution is less dependent on funding than it is on having a plan.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • Assessing need and having clear polices enable staff to act quickly and effectively in a mental health crisis.
  • The counseling center should be housed in a central area with other student services.
  • Referrals to off-campus resources for long-term support is important.

When 22-year-old Katie Meyer killed herself in her dorm room at Stanford University in 2021, it sent shockwaves across the San Francisco Bay Area and the country. One reason was that Meyer was the women's soccer team’s star goalkeeper who had helped Stanford win the national championship two years earlier. The other reason was that she was the fourth Stanford student to die by suicide in just over a year. Stanford officials vowed to improve mental health services at the school, in part by hiring four more counselors and therapists. Eighteen months after Meyer’s death, however, all four positions remained unfilled, and the clinical staff was overwhelmed.[1]

Most colleges offer mental health counseling for students, but this tends to be underfunded, poorly promoted, and difficult to access given staffing shortages. Assessing the need for mental health services, developing a comprehensive strategy for meeting these needs, and having clear policies for what to do if a student is in crisis or hospitalized enables school counselors, medical staff, and administrative leaders to act quickly and effectively to prevent suicides.

At a minimum, the counseling center should be housed in an area with other student services so that it’s visible, accessible, and students don’t feel awkward going there. Beyond that, the center can provide phone consultations, text and chat services, evening and drop-in appointments, and referrals to off-campus resources for long-term and crisis situations. If staffing is a problem, a college can consider using interns and peer counselors linked to the community and provide them with clinical supervision and training.

It’s not just colleges that are experiencing a mental health crisis among students, however. High schools and junior highs are, too—and they don’t have anywhere near the financial resources that a university like Stanford has with its multi-billion-dollar endowment. Fortunately, a significant part of the solution doesn’t depend on finances as much as it depends on planning.

There are three stages in dealing with any crisis. The first is prevention, which involves taking steps to reduce the likelihood of a crisis occurring. The primary focus is risk assessment. In school settings, this means evaluating each student’s mental health, identifying those who now or in the near future may be contemplating suicide, and seeing that they receive appropriate treatment as soon as possible. It’s an ongoing process that requires well-thought-out assessment tools, good training practices, and a competent and confident staff. It also requires staff to ask parents whether their child has access to a firearm or other lethal means.

The second stage is intervention, which is taking action to stop a crisis from escalating and providing first aid or other support to any victims. Intervention starts with getting the facts and assessing the situation, then sharing information among pre-determined, need-to-know individuals. After that, everyone follows established policies for how school personnel respond to in-school and out-of-school suicide attempts, as well as when parents are notified, when law enforcement is summoned, and when students can re-enter school following an incident. Many schools have plans to deal with bullying, but fewer have plans to deal with suicide.

article continues after advertisement

The third stage, postvention, begins when the immediate crisis is over. It includes initiating support services, such as grief counseling. It also includes communicating externally—primarily via the media—using a designated spokesperson who provides key facts, free of judgment. This serves to control rumors and avoid sensationalized reporting. In addition, postvention includes appropriate memorials. All deaths should be treated with reverence but also with messaging that minimizes the possibility of suicide contagion. In this way, postvention becomes prevention, and the cycle starts all over again.

Every institution—public and private—has a role to play in suicide prevention. For most—including schools—it starts with having and following a plan.

If you or someone you love is contemplating suicide, seek help immediately. For help 24/7, dial 988 for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, or reach out to the Crisis Text Line by texting TALK to 741741. To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.
