item.title: Why Parents Protesting Screens in Schools are Right
item.description:
Education

Why Parents Protesting Screens in Schools are Right

Research confirms individual screens in schools are harmful.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • New, plunging test results for U.S. students confirms the trend of recent declines.
  • These educational and cognitive losses coincide with the trend toward increasing screen use in schools.
  • Science tells us how and why screen use erodes attention and learning.
  • Returning to embodied methods of learning is essential to improve educational outcomes.
Source: Shutterstock/standard license

American parents knew there was a problem, and they were right: students’ scores have plunged on the first National Educational Assessment report since the Covid epidemic. Despite mounting parental protests, virtually all of America’s children (96%) regularly use individual laptops or tablets for schoolwork and homework, starting in Kindergarten. We can now see the results of this unprecedented classroom experiment, and they’re dismal: lower test scores in math and reading comprehension and—more disturbingly—an overall decline in cognitive capability. After a hundred years in which each generation scored higher than the last on IQ tests, the trend has reversed and today’s children are losing ground.

How do we know screens are (at least partially) to blame? Because that decline hasn’t occurred in countries where traditional schooling methods are still used, and because the more time children spend interacting with screens, the worse their test outcomes become. But why would this be the case? The answer lies both in the nature of human learning and the nature of computer-based experiences.

Neuroscientists have demonstrated that intelligence and learning are embodied experiences. Compared with typing, writing notes by hand activates more regions of the brain and forces you to actively assess the key points of a lesson. Later, when reviewing those hand-written notes, the sense memory of creating words on a specific part of a specific page is linked to rich contextual understanding of that information — like the tone of a teacher’s voice, the place you were sitting, and which interconnected ideas in your mind at the time. None of these memory cues exist in words floating across a computer screen. The same difference exists between geometry exercises done with a protractor and pencil, compared with clicking a computer button. Research also shows that we retain more when reading from paper than on a computer, because words on-screen lack the fixed spatial location on a page that supports forming memories.

Sacrificing the embodiment necessary for learning isn’t all that happens when education switches from physical materials to screens. Computers and tablets are designed to encourage multi-tasking. But human brains don’t “multi-task.” Instead, when we’re on a computer, our attention rapidly switches between things—the opposite of the concentrated focus that facilitates learning. Studies show that even short-term engagement with an extensively hyperlinked environment (like online shopping) reduces sustained attention after coming offline. The more time children spend on screens—in school and at home—the more likely they may be to develop symptoms of Attention Deficit Disorder (ADD). Despite this growing body of evidence, companies like Google, Microsoft, Anthropic, and OpenAI continue to aggressively lobby for increased adoption of their technology by educators and school districts.

article continues after advertisement

Of course, computers do have some place in schools. They can effectively be used in class during limited periods of time for specific research projects, with students taking hand-written notes and presenting their findings in their own words. Schools should also fund courses on typing, distinguishing reliable from unreliable online sources, using office software, and computer programming. However, expecting that simply using computers for homework and test-taking will lead to computer literacy is like assuming students will learn to be mechanics by riding the bus.

While increased use of screens for learning was necessary during Covid school closures, that era is over. Returning to pencil and paper, embodied learning is essential to combat the use of generative AI chatbots that degrade our ability to think. In the face of parental protests, some school districts, like those in Los Angeles, New York City, and Portland, OR, have recently taken steps to limit student use of screens and AI. However, we must go further and stop spending overstretched school budgets on harmful technology and remove one-to-one computers from classrooms. Instead of subjecting children to this failed experiment, we must return to methods of education that work with, not against, millions of years of human evolution.
